The unusually named candidate for the center-left Ahora Nación party won 34% of the vote. According to local media, the top three candidates were separated by just 42 votes.

Simeon’s candidate application form gives few details (and none about his name), apart from the fact that he manages the Simeon Sac Investment Group.

There have been other politicians called Hitler. In 2018, also in Peru, Hitler beat Lenin in another mayoral race for the district of Yúngar, when Hitler Guesclin Alba Sánchez defeated Lenin Vladimir Rodríguez Valverde.

“I’m the good Hitler,” Alba told broadcasters on the campaign trail, local media reported.

In Namibia, Adolf Hitler Uunona last year won his fifth local election in a row. “As a child I saw it as a totally normal name,” he told the BBC.

]]> en EU’s new list of critical mineral projects focuses on clean energy metals https://www.politico.eu/article/eus-new-list-of-critical-mineral-projects-focuses-on-clean-energy-metals/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 09 Oct 2026 08:07:39 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9134777 BRUSSELS — The European Commission announced a new list of 46 projects Friday in a bid to diversify away from China’s grip on raw materials and establish its own mineral sovereignty.

The projects span extraction, processing, recycling, and substitution for raw materials to supply the EU’s defense, automotive, clean tech and technology industries.

Many of the projects are designed to support electrification and the battery value chain. Lithium, nickel, cobalt, manganese and graphite — the five key battery metals used in electric vehicles and grid-scale batteries — dominate the list. Copper and aluminum, conductors that are used in anything involving electricity, also figure prominently.

Through these projects, Brussels wants to meet its targets under the Critical Raw Materials Act, which, by 2030, the bloc aims to mine at least 10%, process 40% and recycle 25% of its own needs, while sourcing no more than 65% of any one material at any processing stage from a single non-EU country.

The list covers 15 of the 17 “strategic minerals” under the act, which the bloc needs to deliver these targets on each one.

Friday’s announcement is the second batch of strategic projects listed under the act, after the EU rolled out its first list in March 2025, featuring 47 projects and 13 non-EU country projects. The majority of those projects are behind schedule however, highlighting the complexity of getting critical mineral projects up and running.

“With the projects selected in 2025 and 2026, we could now fully meet our European extraction target for lithium, nickel, rare earths, magnesium and tungsten,” said the bloc’s industry chief, Stéphane Séjourné. “We could also meet our processing target for lithium and rare earths. And our recycling target for lithium, cobalt and rare earths.”

With over 170 applications received, the 46 projects span 16 EU member countries: Belgium, Bulgaria, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Slovakia, Spain, Romania and Sweden.

“Exactly one year ago, we experienced firsthand why this matters. On Oct. 9, 2025, China announced new export restrictions on rare earths,” said Séjourné. Those export controls are due to expire in January.

The “strategic project” label is meant to provide faster permitting and help secure public and private finance, with permitting deadlines of 27 months for mines and 15 months for processing and recycling projects.

The Commission will also announce strategic projects in non-EU countries later this year.

The shortfall raises the prospect of a winter of soaring power bills and forced energy saving measures if the bloc fails to find adequate supplies elsewhere.

As the war in Iran continues to disrupt global energy supplies, the EU faces an overall shortfall this winter of up to 14 billion cubic meters of natural gas — around 7% of the bloc’s demand and enough to power between 10 and 12 million European households, according to a report by the Institution for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis, a U.S.-based energy think tank.

Those conclusions are echoed in a key report by a top European body of gas network operators that was presented to national energy officials on Thursday.

Natural gas is used widely to heat Europe’s buildings, power its industry and generate its electricity. But the EU’s gas reserves have fallen to their lowest level for the time of year since records began in 2011, at just above 70%, after high prices made it more attractive for traders to sell gas in the summer rather than store it for later use in the winter.

With gas prices at near-four-year highs and supply constrained due to the U.S.-Israeli war in the Middle East, Europe has limited supply options if the coming winter proves as cold as the last, IEEFA found.

While that doesn’t necessarily mean the bloc will run out of gas, it does mean there could be 7 billion fewer cubic meters of stored gas to draw upon. That could force countries to buy gas at high prices on increasingly volatile global markets, or even require consumers to cut demand if fresh supplies are unavailable.

The EU’s record-low reserves leave the bloc “with less of a buffer” against global supply disruptions, leaving it “vulnerable to price spikes,” Ana Jaller-Makarewicz, IEEFA’s lead European energy analyst, said in a statement. If countries are forced to exhaust stocks this year, that would also leave them with more to refill next year, continuing the feedback loop of low reserves and higher prices, she added.

The same risks were outlined in a 2026-2027 winter supply outlook published Thursday by the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas (ENTSO-G), an association of gas operators. The report warns that if imports of liquefied natural gas are limited or even “optimal” in the context of a cold winter, storage levels could fall as low as 11%, a baseline needed for strategic reserves that can’t be easily tapped into.

If countries hope to restore their reserves to 30% by the end of winter — or else face increased exposure to future cold spells — volumes equivalent to 7% of the demand will either have to be curtailed or simply withheld from consumers, ENTSO-G warns.

Part of that pressure comes from a looming EU-wide ban on long-term supply contracts for Russian LNG, due to take effect in January, which will reduce European gas imports by an additional 7 billion cubic meters, according to the IEEFA report. Russian gas has been historically used to offset “swings in demand” over the winter, it said. “Now Europe depends on storage to get through winter.”

To make matters worse, the IEEFA report argues, gas demand over winter has crept up in the past two years, while imports to the bloc have flatlined. That’s left the EU leaning harder on its reserves over the winter period, with net drawdowns rising to 22.6 billion cubic meters in January this year, up from 18.8 billion cubic meters in January 2025 and 17.8 billion cubic meters in January 2024.

The alternative would be to import fresh LNG, a seaborne fuel that the EU increasingly sources from the U.S. But at current prices, importing the lost volumes would cost Europeans an additional €3 billion, a 12% rise over what the same volume would have cost last year, on top of already sky-high prices, according to the report. U.S. LNG production is also near full capacity, meaning those additional imports would further squeeze supply, Jaller-Makarewicz told POLITICO.

To some, a rise in prices is more likely. While ENTSO-G’s tight market scenario assumes a “global deficit” that sees available LNG imports into Europe reduced by 20%, Laurent Ruseckas, a senior gas market analyst at S&P Global Energy, argues that reserves can only ever fall so low, “since a rapid drawdown early in winter will drive up prices,” drawing cargoes to Europe from Asia.

“There is not much demand to destroy in Europe,” he added, pointing out that the war in Ukraine already destroyed 20% of the bloc’s industrial demand. “And it didn’t come back.”

Warum Deutschland jetzt aus Worten Gesetze machen muss https://www.politico.eu/sponsored-content/berechenbare-risiken-unberechenbare-politik-warum-deutschland-jetzt-aus-worten-gesetze-machen-muss/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 09 Oct 2026 03:00:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=sponsored-content&p=9122126 In der Ökonomie gibt es eine fundamentale Unterscheidung, die für das Verständnis unternehmerischer Entscheidungen zentral ist: Das Risiko und die Ungewissheit. Risiko lässt sich berechnen, einpreisen, managen. Man kennt die Spielregeln – auch wenn man nicht weiß, wie das Spiel ausgeht. Ungewissheit hingegen entzieht sich jeder Formel, weil sich die Spielregeln selbst immer wieder verändern.

Wer neue Technologien entwickelt, Produktionskapazitäten aufbaut und langfristige Zukunftsprojekte anstößt, ist bereit, Risiken einzugehen. In kaum einer Branche zeigt sich das deutlicher als in der forschenden Pharma- und Biotech-Industrie. Denn bis ein neues Medikament bei Patientinnen und Patienten in der Versorgung ankommt, vergehen 10 bis 15 Jahre milliardenschwerer Forschung und Entwicklung. Und die Wahrscheinlichkeit, auf dem Weg zu scheitern, liegt bei über 90%. Mit diesem Risiko können wir umgehen. Es ist fester Bestandteil unseres Geschäftsmodells, das auf Innovation ausgerichtet ist. Es ist auch Voraussetzung für die bahnbrechenden Fortschritte, die in der Medizin in den letzten Jahren erzielt wurden.

Was Zukunftsentscheidungen jedoch lähmt: Ungewissheit durch politische Sprunghaftigkeit.

Wer Zukunftsversprechen formuliert, im Alltag der Gesetzgebung aber vor allem den Rotstift an Innovation und Fortschritt ansetzt, konterkariert jegliche Industriepolitik und erstickt Vertrauen im Keim – da hilft das stärkste Signal nicht mehr.

Genau diese erleben wir in der politischen Diskussion zuletzt zu oft. Genau diese Sprunghaftigkeit haben wir als forschende Gesundheitsindustrie in Deutschland in den letzten Monaten in aller Deutlichkeit zu spüren bekommen. Auf der einen Seite ein ambitioniertes Bekenntnis zum Pharmastandort Deutschland im Koalitionsvertrag – eine Pharmastrategie unter der Regie des Bundeskanzleramtes. Ein starkes Signal!

Auf der anderen Seite dann aber gravierende Eingriffe in bestehende Spielregeln. Eine Gesetzgebung, die einzig und allein darauf abzielt, wieder einmal Finanzlöcher auf Seiten der Kassen zu stopfen – maßgeblich auf Kosten der Industrie durch künstliche Preisdeckel und Zwangsrabatte. Wer Zukunftsversprechen formuliert, im Alltag der Gesetzgebung aber vor allem den Rotstift an Innovation und Fortschritt ansetzt, konterkariert jegliche Industriepolitik und erstickt Vertrauen im Keim – da hilft das stärkste Signal nicht mehr.

Ein gefährlicher Dominoeffekt

Wenn Vertrauen schwindet, explodiert ein Industriestandort nicht mit einem lauten Knall. Vielmehr setzt eine leise Kettenreaktion ein, bei der ein Dominostein den nächsten umwirft. Und klar ist: Die ersten Steine des Gesundheits- und Forschungsstandorts Deutschland sind längst gekippt – mit direkten Folgen für Wirtschaft, Versorgung und Sicherheit:

  • Abfluss von Risikokapital: Milliardenschweres Risikokapital ist global mobil und fließt in jene Märkte, in denen Innovation ein erfolgreiches Geschäftsmodell sein kann. Schon heute vereinen die USA über 50 Prozent des weltweiten Pharmamarktes auf sich, auf Deutschland entfallen lediglich 4-5 Prozent. Mit Regulierung, die Innovation entwertet, verliert Deutschland weiter an Attraktivität und private Investitionen fließen in Zukunft noch häufiger in jene Märkte, die mit strategischer Konsequenz innovationsfreundliche Rahmenbedingungen schaffen.
  • Verlust an Forschung und Innovationskraft: Wo Kapital abwandert, schrumpft auch die wissenschaftliche Substanz. Der europäische Anteil an der globalen Pharma-Forschung ist in den letzten Jahrzehnten drastisch von über 40 auf knapp 30 Prozent gefallen; der Anteil an klinischen Studien hat sich binnen einer Dekade auf 9 Prozent halbiert. Auch Deutschland ist längst zurückgefallen: Im Global Innovation Index der WIPO zählen wir erstmals nicht mehr zu den zehn innovationsstärksten Volkswirtschaften der Welt.
  • Gefährdung der medizinischen Versorgung: Ein Markt, der Innovation nicht fair honoriert, ist unattraktiv für medizinische Durchbrüche. Schon heute sehen wir, dass Deutschland seine Rolle als globaler Versorgungspionier verliert: Jedes dritte in den USA neu zugelassene Medikament erreicht Patientinnen und Patienten in Deutschland nicht mehr. Besonders alarmierend: Bei zwei Dritteln dieser Therapien handelt es sich um Präparate mit anerkannt hohem Innovationsstatus.
  • Verlust von Souveränität: In Zeiten geopolitischer Umbrüche und fragiler Lieferketten sind medizinische Schlüsseltechnologien längst zu einer Währung für nationale Resilienz geworden. Wer Forschung und Produktion im eigenen Land vernachlässigt, gibt Handlungsspielräume auf und gerät bei der Versorgung der eigenen Bevölkerung in gefährliche Abhängigkeiten.

Chance auf einen Perspektivwechsel

Zukunftsfähigkeit, Innovationskraft und Souveränität lassen sich nicht durch kurzsichtiges Flickwerk verteidigen. Um den Dominoeffekt, der unseren Gesundheitsstandort erfasst hat, zu stoppen, braucht es jetzt ein Umdenken; weg von Verteilungsdebatten hin zu einem verlässlichen Bekenntnis zu Innovationen.

Erstmals wird medizinischer Fortschritt nicht mehr einseitig von der Kostenseite gedacht, sondern daran gemessen, was die forschende Gesundheitsindustrie durch Forschung, Entwicklung, Produktion und hochwertige Arbeitsplätze für unser Land leistet.

Dazu gehört auch, dass wir uns ehrlich machen: Die finanzielle Schieflage der Kassen entsteht durch strukturelle Ineffizienzen im System, nicht durch medizinischen Fortschritt. Ganz im Gegenteil: Innovative Medizin ist kein Kostenfaktor, sondern eine Investition in die Zukunft. Der konsequente Einsatz modernster Diagnostik, digitaler Prozesse und innovativer Therapien könnte schon heute jährlich über 40 Milliarden Euro freisetzen – direkt im Gesundheitssystem und indirekt als positiver Effekt auf Wirtschaft, Wachstum und Wohlstand.

Die Politik hat jetzt die Chance, einen Perspektivwechsel einzuleiten. Eine Expertenkommission hat jüngst konkret vorgeschlagen, wie Unternehmen, die in Deutschland investieren, von einem Teil – wohlgemerkt: nur einem Teil – jener zusätzlichen Belastungen ausgenommen werden können, die mit dem GKV-Beitragssatzstabilisierungsgesetz eingeführt wurden. Diese Vorschläge zur Verknüpfung des Herstellerabschlags mit einer sogenannten Standortklausel liegen nun auf dem Tisch. Und sie sind schon bemerkenswert: Erstmals wird medizinischer Fortschritt nicht mehr einseitig von der Kostenseite gedacht, sondern daran gemessen, was die forschende Gesundheitsindustrie durch Forschung, Entwicklung, Produktion und hochwertige Arbeitsplätze für unser Land leistet. Ein Ansatz, der Industriepolitik, Sozialpolitik und Geopolitik endlich zusammendenkt.

Denn erst dann sendet die Bundesregierung die notwendige politische Verbindlichkeit.

Dabei wird uns keineswegs etwas geschenkt: Die Kassen werden mit einem erhöhten Herstellerabschlag von 15,5% weiterhin auf Rekordniveau durch die Industrie gestützt – Unternehmen, die nachweislich vor Ort Werte schaffen, Arbeitsplätze sichern und Forschung verankern, erhalten lediglich die Chance, die zusätzlichen Belastungen zu reduzieren. Das ist kein Geschenk – sondern die Korrektur einer massiven Fehlsteuerung. Eine vorausschauende, ressortübergreifende Standortstrategie hätte von vornherein auf positive Anreize gesetzt, statt bestehende Strukturen zu schwächen. Umso wichtiger ist es, dass daraus nun schnell ein wirksames, unbürokratisches Gesetz wird – und dass weitere Schritte folgen. Denn erst dann sendet die Bundesregierung die notwendige politische Verbindlichkeit. Denn milliardenschwere Investitionsentscheidungen in die Zukunft Deutschlands folgen keinen Kommissionspapieren – sondern verlässlichen Taten, die die Grundlage für eine Pharma-Strategie werden können, die Deutschlands Wettbewerbsfähigkeit wiederherstellt und den internationalen Herausforderungen gerecht wird.

Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali won the central London House of Commons seat with 12,292 votes, a majority of 3,364 over Green Leader Polanski, who came second with 8,928.

The poll was triggered when Keir Starmer stood down as an MP last month after being ousted as U.K. prime minister.

It is an early boost for Starmer’s replacement Andy Burnham, who has shifted the ruling Labour Party to the left since taking charge and toughened the U.K.’s stance on Israel amid criticism that his predecessor’s response to the war in Gaza was flat-footed.

And it has triggered a round of soul-searching in the left-wing Greens, already fractious over a deeply controversial motion on Zionism passed at their party conference. The party had been troubling Labour in the polls under Polanski, but has now fallen short of a high-profile target.

The north London seat has been held by Labour since its creation in 1983 — but the Greens poured significant resources into trying to get their leader elected.

Abdi-Wali got 45% of the vote – down four points on Labour’s 2024 general election result. Polanski won 33% of the votes cast — a 22-point leap on the party’s 2024 result, but still some way short of taking the traditionally-safe Labour seat.

A defeated Polanski – who had gambled on getting a toehold in parliament to boost the Greens’ profile – insisted he would stay on as party leader, telling broadcasters: “I’ve taken a loss tonight, but our movement is so much bigger than one election or one motion.”

Polanski told Sky News Friday he is “disappointed” by the result, but put his defeat down to voters wanting to “give Andy Burnham a chance.”

He argued the Green Party’s fortunes have changed because Labour has moved closer to Green positions. “We’ve now got a different prime minister who is in a honeymoon, who is talking a lot of the language I’ve been talking about for the past year,” he said. “So I see that as a result.”

Abdi-Wali, who arrived in the U.K. as a child refugee from Somalia and has faced attacks on her background from the right-wing Reform UK party, meanwhile said her victory was “deeply personal” and vowed to work with Burnham to tackle homelessness. She said she wants to see Thames Water — the giant private water company that serves her constituents — brought into public ownership.

U.K. polling expert John Curtice said the Holborn result is “still by far and away [the Greens’] second best ever result in a parliamentary by-election” —  but warned the Greens are “now operating in a more politically competitive environment.”

“The trouble is that when you manage to bring down an unpopular leader of your opponents, you’ve then got to deal with the consequences, which in this case is that Labour have put in place somebody who is more popular,” Curtice said of the party’s boast that it helped persuade Labour MPs to oust Starmer in favor of the more left-wing Burnham.

A Labour official said voters who were not giving the party a hearing earlier in the year were now listening again.

Curtice pointed out that while Labour is enjoying a substantial Burnham bounce they are “still short of where they were in 2024.”

Green dissent

Polanski’s defeat also comes as Green Party divisions spill into the open after members passed a controversial motion declaring Zionism to be a form of racism at their party conference last weekend.

One London councillor said the move had been  “electoral suicide,” and shortly after polls closed Thursday the veteran former MP Caroline Lucas told the BBC that Polanski, who did not attend the vote in Brighton, “should have been there” and should now “show the leadership that was frankly missing on Sunday.” 

Asked if Polanski should stand down, Lucas — a former party leader who was the first Green MP to be elected to the House of Commons — said: “I think let’s just see what happens in the coming days and weeks.”

Pushed on Lucas’ criticisms, Polanski told Sky News Friday that she is a “significant figure,” but that members are “entitled to have different opinions.”

A senior Green local politician allied to Polanski, granted anonymity to discuss internal matters, said: “You can’t really force a coup” in the Green Party — highlighting that a leadership election is not due for another year.

And his rival for the Green candidacy Hamza Chowdhury — a Green councillor in Camden — said at the count: “This is a f*cking win mate. Labour might be celebrating now but wait till 2029 when we wipe the floor with them.”

Polanski did not say Friday if he agrees with party members who voted for the Zionism motion, which has been sharply criticized by Israel, rival British parties, and the chief of the Jewish Greens, when questioned at the by-election count.

He told broadcasters:  “As I say, the displacement of the Palestinian people, the genocide, is clearly racist.”

The dispute spilled out onto the airwaves Friday morning as the party reflected on its defeat.

Labour Party Chair Bridget Phillipson punched the bruise, accusing the Greens of holding “British Jews to a higher standard than we would expect of others.” She said the party needs to “distance themselves from this motion.” 

Green peer Jenny Jones told Times Radio that the Zionism row marked a “rather big blip” — but insisted Polanski would stay on for at least another year. “We don’t do things in the Green Party the way that other political parties do,” she said. “We don’t depose leaders by gossip and criticism. We actually try to work through things.”

But Vivien Lichtenstein, a veteran of the party who chairs the internal Jewish Greens group, accused the leader of a dereliction of duty over the motion. Pressed on whether Polanski should stay in post, she told Times Radio bluntly: “No, I think he should resign.”

This column has, once again, been overlooked for the Nobel Prize in Literature — although there’s still hope for the Peace Prize.

Asked by Declassified if it could justify this blatant discrimination, the Nobel committee hung up the phone.

Politicians can, of course, make great writers, and several have won Nobel’s literature prize, including Britain’s Winston Churchill in 1953, and Peru’s Mario Vargas Llosa in 2010. The latter — who ran for president in 1990 — won the prize “for his cartography of structures of power and his trenchant images of the individual’s resistance, revolt, and defeat.” But has he ever referred to British Conservative grandee Jacob Rees-Mogg as a “Haunted Pencil”? No, he has not.

There are, however, a lot of very bad books written by politicians.

Former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson — very much the “Winston Churchill if you ordered him off Temu” — published a book in 2004 called “Seventy-Two Virgins — A Comedy of Errors” (the last four words also being the summary of his Covid policy) about a terrorist group targeting the U.S. president on a visit to London. It was described in the Guardian some 15 years later — after Johnson became prime minister — as ” sexist, racist, fundamentally undiplomatic.”

But the undisputed king when it comes to politicians letting out their inner writer is France.

In 2023, Bruno Le Maire, then the country’s economy and finance minister, published the novel “Fugue Américaine,” which drew instant criticism and mockery, mainly because of an explicit sex scene (unhappy French people were quick to point out that they had been screwed by the government for years).

Then there’s Marlène Schiappa, former government minister and writer of raunchy books under the pen name Marie Minelli, with titles such as “Osez les sexfriends,” “Sexe, mensonge et banlieues chaudes” and “Comment transformer votre mec en Brad Pitt en 30 jours.” When she was junior social affairs minister, Schiappa appeared on the cover of Playboy, although she was not naked in the magazine (great news for those who buy Playboy only for the articles). 

Former President Valéry Giscard d’Estaing published several erotic novels, including “La Princesse et le Président,” which features sex scenes set in the presidential palace.

But perhaps the most intriguing of all is current President Emmanuel Macron, whose erotic novel about the early days of his romance with Brigitte has, alas, never seen the light of day. Perhaps he’s keeping it back for political gain and will promise to publish the steamy tome if the people of France promise to vote for a centrist candidate in April’s election.

]]> en ‘Not great, not terrible’: Why nobody trusts Russia to tell the truth about plague https://www.politico.eu/article/plague-russia-laboratory-truth-trust-transparency-health-risk/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 08 Oct 2026 21:17:37 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9132407 As whispers circulate of plague in faraway Siberia, it’s worth remembering that Russian obfuscation is so ingrained that it’s become a meme.

In HBO’s dramatized 2019 series about the nuclear disaster at Chernobyl, a Russian atomic scientist scoffs at a radiation reading that suggests a major calamity is taking place. 

“Not great, not terrible,” says the fictionalized version of Anatoly Dyatlov, the real-life deputy chief engineer at Chernobyl in April 1986, as he looks at a dosimeter noting 3.6 roentgen per hour, just below a critical radiation level. 

Except that reading was not accurate. Not even close. The nuclear reactor had already exploded and unleashed catastrophic levels of radiation that would go on to cause thousands of cancer-related deaths in the worst nuclear power plant disaster in history.

While dramatized, the scene is emblematic of a long-standing Soviet and Russian desire to downplay critical incidents — and even cover them up. That pattern has flared this week, with senior world health officials, the European Union and U.S. President Donald Trump demanding that Moscow be more transparent about a suspected outbreak of plague in far eastern Russia.

In dark comedic twist in the face of the potential plague, Dyatlov’s dismissive remark is now ubiquitous. Not great, not terrible. 

Into the unknown

The death of a 28-year-old employee at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East last week triggered unease across the globe due to her laboratory work — and a local Russian official linking her death to a case of plague.

Russia was quick to clamp down. Rospotrebnadzor, the country’s national public health agency, said that the employee died from “pneumonia of unknown etiology” and that no microorganisms associated with her work were identified in the patient sample.

Still, Russian health authorities placed nearly 200 people under supervision and local media reported that several hospitals were placed under quarantine. Rospotrebnadzor said Thursday these measures were taken due to “the patient’s professional activities.”

The World Health Organization, which leads global response to international health threats, got in touch with Russian health authorities on Oct. 3. It requested more information using one of the tools laid out in the International Health Regulations, which Russia is signed up to. Under the IHR, countries have 24 hours to respond to the WHO — though Russia sent its response on Oct. 6.

Russian authorities said that “no case of plague had recently been registered in Irkutsk” and “no pathogens of dangerous infectious diseases were detected among any of the contacts.”

As of Thursday, Russian health authorities maintain that there is no “epidemic risk” in the region. Rospotrebnadzor said that it had concluded health inspections and found “no emergency situations involving pathogenic microorganisms.” It had also completed monitoring of 90% of the contacts, without identifying any infections, the agency added. Simultaneously, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov slammed media reports about the case as false and said Russia has been communicating with global health authorities.

Yet the WHO insists there’s still much left unknown about the events inside Russia.

“We don’t know exactly how this person died,” said Maria Van Kerkhove, director of epidemic and pandemic management, during a press briefing Wednesday. “We know that she had pneumonia. We know it was a fatal case. We understand that some laboratory tests have been done. They haven’t found the causative agent. This is why we need more information.”

The WHO said it requested further details on what laboratory tests were conducted, which pathogens were evaluated, which further analyses are being done to determine the patient’s cause of death — if not plague — along with more details on any potential lab incident and the 200 contacts.

Until those questions are answered, it’s impossible for the WHO to conduct a risk assessment.

“We don’t yet have the full picture of this event, and we are not able to conduct a full risk assessment,” said Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the organization’s director-general. “Timely, complete, and transparent information sharing under the international regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks.”

Omertà in Russian

It might be that the cause of death of the 28-year-old lab worker is not, in fact, plague. 

But Russia’s incomplete, late and hazy communication about the case is fomenting fears and uncertainty from Geneva to Brussels to Washington. It would also not be the first time the Kremlin has downplayed or attempted to cover up public health threats.  

That goes beyond the Soviet-era Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant disaster, in what is now northern Ukraine, where the Kremlin was slow to take action and effectively denied the cause of the incident.

In 1979, according to an investigation by U.S. scientists, the Soviet Union covered up a deadly anthrax outbreak in the city of Sverdlovsk, now Yekaterinburg, which killed at least 66 people. Officials said the victims had fallen ill from eating contaminated meat, when in reality they had been exposed to anthrax because of an accident at a secret biological weapons lab.

Russia was also accused of covering up a mysterious 1988 alopecia outbreak in Chernivtsi region, in which more than 175 children lost their hair. Soviet authorities said the children suffered from thallium food poisoning, but later studies raised questions about that, with some suggesting the cause was hydrazine, or acid rain.

Over the years, the Kremlin has also dismissed, downplayed and underreported HIV cases, even while in the middle of a deadly epidemic. And, more recently, during the Covid-19 pandemic, Russia was accused of downplaying coronavirus deaths, particularly at the beginning. 

The tradition extends beyond public health. The 1999 apartment block bombings, the 2000 sinking of the Kursk submarine and the 2014 downing of Malaysia Airlines flight MH17 by Kremlin-backed separatists all raised questions over Russia’s public messaging and commitment to transparency.

Talks with Putin

The EU and the U.S. are monitoring the Irkutsk situation closely, with both seemingly growing impatient with Russia’s communication. 

“The whole world is waiting for the information from Russia,” said European Commission spokesperson Eva Hrncirova on Thursday.

“Russia should make information about the plague available as soon as possible,” she told reporters. “We need information from Russia. It’s linked to the Russian membership in the WHO Europe, sharing timely, precise, exact information so that the experts can assess the situation, because [it] can have cross-border implications.”

The European Commission’s directorate-general for health and food safety is planning to send a technical letter to Russia asking for more information, a Commission spokesperson confirmed.

In the meantime, Russia’s “patchy” communication is dangerous, said a Commission official, granted anonymity to speak candidly on the matter.

“This fuels speculation into all directions. It also renders preventive [and] precautionary action difficult, if not even meaningless,” the official said. These types of events happen all the time, but there is usually an exchange with the WHO and health authorities, the person added. “The lack of precise [and] reliable info is logically reducing adequate good preparedness.”

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday urged Russia to share more information, adding that it would be “irresponsible” to speculate until then. The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that the U.S. sent a formal diplomatic message to Russia requesting more information about the woman’s death and reminding the Kremlin that it has obligations under international law to share information about disease outbreaks in a timely manner.

U.S. President Donald Trump even said Tuesday he had a “call scheduled” with Russian President Vladimir Putin “very soon” to discuss the situation. 

But, by Thursday, the two leaders were yet to talk, with Trump noting that Russia was “not saying much.” 

He still planned to talk to Putin soon, he added.

]]> en EU cyber and science researchers are testing Chinese AI models  https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-cybersecurity-and-science-researchers-are-testing-chinese-ai-models/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 08 Oct 2026 20:54:20 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9124013 BRUSSELS — The European Union’s cybersecurity agency and in-house research center have each begun experimenting with open artificial intelligence models from China, three EU officials have told POLITICO.

The Joint Research Centre (JRC) — the EU’s in-house scientific research center — is evaluating “publicly available open-weight models” originating from China, European Commission spokesperson Maciej Berestecki confirmed. The head of ENISA, the bloc’s agency responsible for cybersecurity, also said in an interview that his team was now testing Chinese AI.

The experiments with Chinese models at the JRC are part of a broader research project to evaluate artificial intelligence that also includes leading models from the United States and Europe, Berestecki said. “Models from different origins are included in a comparative scientific evaluation of their capabilities, performance, limitations and risks,” he said, adding that the JRC is also looking into their potential scientific applications.

AI safety and security — topics currently under intense scrutiny following a series of incidents in which advanced AI models hacked real-world networks during testing activities — are not the core focus of the JRC’s testing activities, according to a different Commission official, who was granted anonymity to discuss sensitive material.

Open-weight models are those whose core components are publicly released, allowing anyone to run the model and study how it works. China’s approach to AI has leaned more towards open models than the United States. Some major U.S. tech and AI companies, including chips giant NVIDIA, are investing in open-weight models.

Forced to choose

The U.S. and China are locked in a race to dominate in the technology, with Europe largely sitting on the sidelines. Without a viable European frontier model, European private and public organizations may be left to choose between American and Chinese providers for advanced AI applications.

In a recent speech, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen suggested Europe should not try to win the frontier AI race. A top German tech company told POLITICO this week it was dropping Europe’s leading AI lab Mistral in favor of open-source Chinese models.

The JRC has not entered into any “bespoke access” or licensing negotiations with the relevant Chinese developers, Berestecki said. The models are run on the center’s “secure, on-premises scientific infrastructure” and the Commission is not intending to use Chinese models for its own purposes, he added.

EU cyber agency ENISA — which has gained access to advanced models from top U.S. AI firms Anthropic, OpenAI and Google — is also experimenting with “a couple” of open-weight Chinese models, its executive director Juhan Lepassaar confirmed in an interview on Wednesday. 

JRC and ENISA have been tasked with working together to set up an AI testing platform under a recent EU action plan on AI and cyber, the European Commission’s attempt to respond to the growing concerns after a series of incidents involving AI systems breaking out of testing environments and breaking into other organizations’ digital systems.

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Fri, 09 Oct 2026 09:20:36 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 Agrochemical lobbyists are defending a toxic model of agriculture that is heading for collapse https://euobserver.com/241450/agrochemical-lobbyists-are-defending-a-toxic-model-of-agriculture-that-is-heading-for-collapse/ Fri, 09 Oct 2026 09:06:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241450 As pesticide lobbyists dominate a key hearing in Strasbourg, the EU risks locking farmers and citizens into a costly, chemical-dependent food system that poisons water, fuels disease and drains billions in EU subsidies away from real sustainable farming.]]> Last week, EU member states reached a common position on the European Commission Omnibus X ‘Food and Feed’ proposal, in a bid to simplify regulation of pesticides. In reality, however, it will weaken protection against pesticides’ negative effects in Europe. The proposal pleases the chemical industry but goes against the wishes of a vast majority of citizens and many scientists who value people’s health, clean drinking water and biodiversity.

A hearing in the European Parliament on 3 September highlighted the real problem. Under the guise of a ‘discussion with experts’ in the field of health and environment, the parliament handed the megaphone to lobbyists representing a broken, toxic agricultural model.

Representatives of industrial agriculture – sugar beet, apple and cereal growers – parroted industry arguments, justifying their demands to stop banning pesticides that are toxic to public health, the environment and pollute our water resources.

Despite Europe witnessing massive droughts, extreme heatwaves leading to countless deaths, wildfires destroying biodiversity, and devastating crop losses, it seems that a significant share of MEPs are ready and willing to accelerate the degradation of European’s wellbeing and natural resources. 

Listening to them raises a fundamental question: Do farmers truly want to rely on a cocktail of toxic chemicals to maximise yields at low market prices, destroying their own health and local ecosystems in the process? Or do they wish to make an honest living, producing quality food in balance with nature for a fair income?

Read more

Deadlock on EU pesticides bill after scientists call for pause

CAP subsidies

To better grasp this contradiction, we must look at what is actually at stake here.

Agrochemical corporations seek their share of the Common Agriculture Policy (CAP) cake – a colossal €58bn budget, accounting for one third of the EU’s total budget.

Their own survival is reliant on keeping as many farmers as possible dependent on pesticides, fertilisers and industrial seeds. By diverting public CAP funds through farmers into the pockets of their shareholders, these companies ensure their long-term profitability.

Many farmers’ unions also represent agri-cooperatives that profit significantly from selling pesticides, which raises questions about whether they truly represent farmers’ long-term interests, or those of the pesticide industry.

Since the European Commission published its ‘simplification’ proposal in December 2025, proponents of pesticide-intensive farming have presented a series of flawed arguments that in fact reveal the dead-end to which intensive agriculture has led us.

Read more

Did Europe’s ‘summer of truth’ push climate up von der Leyen’s agenda? Yes, but there were some shocking omissions

Firstly, farmers’ organisations complain about a “lack of pesticide substances” on the market.

Currently around 450 different pesticide active substances are approved in the EU, from insecticides to fungicides, and herbicides. If 450 different options are insufficient, does this not signal an unhealthy addiction rather than a shortage?

Lobbyist groups, furthermore, claim that pest resistance to synthetic pesticides would inevitably lead to dramatic yield losses and hunger, arguing for even more pesticides with diverse modes of action.

And yet, according to scientific research, the  multiple chemical strategy that has been applied for more than 40 years is the very cause of the appearance of resistance. This problem cannot be solved with the mindset that caused it. The only scientific solution is, therefore, not more chemistry but prevention, and the use of alternative methods.

Thousands of farmers across the EU and the rest of the world are already proving this by switching towards Integrated Pest Management (a strategy for low-pesticide-input pest management) or organic practices to reduce pesticide inputs.

Who bares the cost

The call to keep all pesticides on the market – and potentially even use some of the banned ones –  serves only the short-term interests of the pesticide industry, not of the farmers.

Destroying soil life – the basis of soil fertility – with chemicals, and killing insect populations that naturally control pests and pollinate crops, jeopardises the very basis of farming and long-term food security.

Read more

Europe’s children will inherit public-health crisis from new EU pesticide approvals

The societal costs of this pesticide-dependent model are staggering. Citizens are the ones who bear the healthcare costs for chronic diseases such as cancer and Parkinson’s, which impact not only farmers but also residents of agricultural areas.

We face water pollution that has become nearly impossible to remediate. Fewer pollinators means fewer healthy fruit and vegetables. These ‘externalities’ far outweigh any short-term benefits.

This is the reason why the Paris and Munich water companies financially support farmers in protecting the groundwater, because doing so is up to 45 times cheaper than depollution.

In the meantime, the agrochemical industry enjoys huge profits from pesticide sales, largely supported by CAP subsidies, while society foots the bill for the damage. It is indeed a perfect business model…for them.

Lobbyist circus

The spectacle witnessed in the alleged House of European Democracy is testament to the state of our political world; one that is dominated by corporate interests over citizens and farmers’ wellbeing.

We witnessed the desperate battle of a toxic agricultural model that struggles to survive, and resists being replaced by sustainable farming methods.

The lobbyist speakers in the European Parliament hearing more or less gave the diagnosis to the current pesticide-intensive agricultural system: it is simply broken. 

Citizens have repeatedly expressed their concern on the impact of pesticides on their health and biodiversity. They have also expressed the need that public support for agriculture serves the common good.

The pesticide Omnibus X proposal is merely an attempt to maintain a detrimental status quo that favours the pesticides industry.

With the 1968 Mansholt Plan Europe created a blueprint for the intensification of agriculture.

What is needed now is a new blueprint for a system which financially supports farmers to implement practices that improve soil and plant health, favour beneficial insects, accelerate the availability of alternatives to pesticides such as biocontrol products, and rapidly phase out toxic synthetic pesticides to protect our health, water resources and biodiversity.

Only then can we ensure a sustainable future for European agriculture and our children. Only then, will a greater share of the CAP remain in the hands of farmers who feed us and protect our nature.

]]> Listen: What would a coalition of right and far-right in Spain mean for Europe? https://euobserver.com/241939/listen-what-would-a-coalition-of-right-and-far-right-in-spain-mean-for-europe/ Fri, 09 Oct 2026 08:32:45 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241939 Spain is heading for early elections, after Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap vote last week. According to current polls, the conservative People's Party, or PP, is ahead of Sánchez's Socialists, while Vox is also making significant gains. What would happen if they governed together?]]>

Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

Find the full transcript below: 

Spain is heading for early elections, after prime minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap vote last week. According to current polls, the conservative People’s Party, or PP, is ahead of Sánchez’s Socialists, while Vox is also making significant gains.

So, what would happen if the PP and Vox decided to govern together? And what would that mean for Europe? 

Let’s start with the numbers. According to Politico’s poll of polls, the PP, the conservative right-wing party, is currently polling first, at around 34 percent. The Socialists of the PSOE are at around 26 percent, and the far-right party Vox at around 18 percent.

The Socialists already came second in the last general election, in 2023. The PP won the most seats, but it couldn’t form a government. Pedro Sánchez eventually secured enough support from other parties, including the left-wing Sumar, to remain prime minister.

Read more

Spain’s 54-day sprint to the polls: can Sánchez’s housing gamble stop the far-right from entering into government?

This time, the balance could be different. If the current polling were reflected in the election result, the PP and Vox could have enough seats to form a government together. PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo has said he could negotiate with Vox.

And this would not be completely new in Spain. The PP and Vox are already governing together in four Spanish regions: Extremadura, Aragon, Castilla y León and Andalusia.

Now, would that mean Spain would have  a government with Vox ministers? One possibility would be a government led by the PP, with Vox supporting it from outside, without taking ministerial positions. That’s what we’ve seen in Sweden, for example.

But what seems more and more likely is that Vox would become part of the government itself. The Vox MEP José Buxadé told Politico a few weeks ago that if his party negotiates a coalition with the PP, it would seek ministerial positions proportional to the number of votes it receives.

According to Politico, based on current polling, that could mean a third of ministers coming from Vox. So, what would this mean for Europe and for Spain? A lot.

Spain is currently one of the EU countries where the government has taken relatively progressive positions on issues such as migration, climate policy and social policy.

A change of government would therefore give more weight to the right in the European Council. That could be particularly important on migration, but also on economic files.

And then there is climate policy. Vox has called for the abolition of the European Green Deal, arguing that environmental policies have harmed employment and Spain’s energy policy.

Something that is very much contradicted by the fact that Spain is one of the European countries that has been particularly resilient during the energy crisis, thanks to its renewable energy.

So a change in climate policy could have consequences not only for Spain, but also for the EU’s wider energy transition.

And there could be another major change: foreign policy. Pedro Sánchez has been one of the more outspoken European leaders on the war in Gaza. Spain has taken a particularly critical position towards Israel and has recognised a Palestinian state.

Vox takes a very different position. The party strongly supports Israel and has called for European funding to the Palestinian Authority to be suspended.

The Spanish election is still several weeks away, so we don’t yet know whether the PP and Vox will actually be able to form a government, or what form such an agreement would take.

But if they do, Spain’s position in Europe could change quite significantly.

]]> Orbán channelled public money into propaganda through Hungarian billionaire Lőrinc Mészáros (Day 150 of the Tisza government) https://euobserver.com/241773/orban-channelled-public-money-into-propaganda-through-hungarian-billionaire-lorinc-meszaros-day-150-of-the-tisza-government/ Fri, 09 Oct 2026 08:04:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241773 Internal documents show how a top Orbán-era rail contractor showered Megafon influencers with billions of forints.]]> More than a year ago, we launched our Hungary Briefing, a weekly round-up of the election campaign. Since the historic vote in April to remove Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz government, the series has followed the new Tisza administration and its first moves in office. This week’s topics:

  • How Viktor Orbán used Lőrinc Mészáros.
  • According to Orbán, they deliberately did not give money to the liberals.
  • Orbán’s brother also has a gold-convoy case.
  • A wealth tax is coming.
  • Support for Hungarian media beyond the borders.
  • This week’s opinion polls: slight drop for Tisza, strong support for the Olympics

How Viktor Orbán used Lőrinc Mészáros.

The investigative outlet Direkt36 revealed important details about the links between Lőrinc Mészáros’s companies and Orbán-era propaganda in a new series of articles. The investigators obtained internal documents from a company called V-Híd, which showed that the firm belonging to the Mészáros portfolio paid out several billion forints between 2022 and 2026 to influencers in the Megafon network.

The oligarch was not stingy.

V-Híd is one of the most important and most profitable companies in the Mészáros empire, primarily engaged in railway construction. It owes its success almost entirely to the fact that it won huge public procurement contracts under Fidesz governments.

In recent years, V-Híd has become the dominant player in railway construction in Hungary, pushing out its competitors. Enormous dividends have been taken out of the company by the Mészáros clan (most recently, despite weaker results, 10 billion forints, or around €25m).

The Direkt36 article also reveals that Orbán-era propaganda was financed directly from the company’s revenue. Donation contracts were leaked showing that V-Híd regularly sent hundreds of millions of forints as “gifts” to Megafon. In 2024 alone, they sent 3 billion forints (around €7.6m at the time) in support to the influencer network.

The path of public money to propaganda

The formula was very simple: through public procurement, the government stuffed the Mészáros group’s companies with public money, and part of the revenue generated was channelled to the propaganda machine.

From 2020, Megafon was a key communication channel for Fidesz, where well-known influencers conveyed the party’s messages and huge sums were spent on online advertising.

The money won through public tenders did not only go towards financing propaganda. Direkt36 also uncovered luxury perks V-Híd and other Mészáros companies offered their staff.

Read more

The cash convoy case that could be Orbán’s smoking gun, and Magyar’s deputy is getting ever more popular (81 days since the elections)

Many would envy V-Híd’s team-building events. In 2024, nine employees of the company travelled by private jet to a château in south-western France, at a cost 62 million forints, or about €150,000, including €500 spent on cigars.

According to Direkt36, V-Híd has spent more than 1 billion forints in total – roughly €2.5m – on foreign trips in recent years.

On one trip to Tajikistan, V-Híd paid out €46,000 – the Central Asian country is a popular destination for exotic hunting excursions, and Mészáros also took part in such a hunting tour.

The Mészáros clan were also keen on yachting and spent money on private jets. One private jet linked to the Mészáros family was used at least once by Orbán himself.

The money did not go to the liberals

Fidesz has tied itself in knots after the arrest of culture minister Balázs Hankó. Hankó is suspected of aggravated breach of fiduciary duty causing particularly significant financial loss, committed in a criminal conspiracy, and the court has placed him in pre-trial detention.

The Hankó case blew up shortly after the elections, when activist Áron Molnár revealed that the National Cultural Fund had disbursed more than 17 billion forints (around €44m) to artists close to Fidesz for the purposes of the party’s campaign.

]]> Video game industry believes EU Kids Act will drive small creators and old games into extinction https://euobserver.com/241743/video-game-industry-believes-eu-kids-act-will-drive-small-creators-and-old-games-into-extinction/ Fri, 09 Oct 2026 07:33:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241743 Campaigners have warned that stringent requirements to adapt games to children by default would prompt the extinction of small games and make costs spiral for developers.]]> A new law aimed at protecting children could kill off old video games and threaten small developers, industry trade groups have warned.

The EU Kids Act was unveiled by commission president Ursula von der Leyen last month as a chance to “give childhood back to our children” and put parents “in the driving seat”.

It would require videogames to be catered to children by default with stringent requirements including an eight-hour nighttime lock-out, a ban on screenshots, and guardian supervision.

Gamers wanting to play the full version of games would have to pass age verification checks to access features, like multi-player tournaments or mystery boxes. 

The European Commission is gathering feedback on the act with respondents quick to criticise the threat posed to videogame makers.

Stop Killing Games, a campaign to protect videogames, has opposed the act.

“This could turn the EU into a pariah state for videogames,” said Ross Scott, the consumer group’s founder. He reckons the regulation could spark a race to update games or deactivate them.

MEPs have also joined in sounding the alarm bell.

Proposed law could kill games

If the law passed, developers would need to make a child mode version of games and gate the full games behind a verification step.

“This is going to bury developers with compliance steps, and a whole lot of cost,” said Scott.

Age verification with zero-knowledge proof (meaning developers cannot collect data) will likely be required. “In practice, providers would likely need to engage a third-party age assurance provider,” also said Lauro Fava, partner at law firm Pinsent Masons.

The Commission’s impact assessment claims that third-party age verification apps would reduce costs, but failed to provide estimates.

Fava called it “strange” that these were missing, and thinks the commission “arguably downplayed” the cost of compliance.

Gamer’s Voice, an advocacy group, asserted that small games would struggle to pay for age-verification and other compliance measures, likely to inlclude game redesigns.

The Kids Act would outlaw features ‘increasing social comparison’ for minors, meaning functions like leaderboards and kill counts could be restricted.

Read more

EU plans Europe‑wide social media age limits, but can Brussels really police Big Tech?

And while the cost to developers is not known, it is feared prices could increase for players.

The wide scope of the draft law means community servers and hobbyist-developed games could be subjected to the new rules. Any game, new or old, would have to follow measures unless strictly offline in a physical format or built only for educational purposes.

And since the rules would apply to games made or consumed in the EU, it is feared game makers could block access to their games on the bloc.

]]> French kitchenware giant Tefal faces legal ultimatum over harmful chemicals, as Europeans’ health at stake https://euobserver.com/241872/french-kitchenware-tefal-faces-legal-ultimatum-over-harmful-chemicals-as-europeans-health-at-stake/ Fri, 09 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241872 Environmental NGOs have threatened to sue the owner of Tefal, a leading French kitchenware company, over failing to phase out forever chemicals from their products, at a high price for consumer health.]]> Environmental NGOs have threatened to sue the owner of Tefal, a leading French kitchenware company, over failing to phase out forever chemicals from their products, at a high price for consumer health.

The organisations allege that Groupe SEB, the parent company of known brands, such as Tefal cookware, Calor irons, and Moulinex kitchen appliances, fails to curtail harmful chemicals in its products.

And the environmentalist groups have threatened to file a lawsuit if the firm fails to makes a change to its policy within three months.

Companies have a duty to identify and address the impact of their work and products under the French law, for instance the pollution they cause or human rights they might violate.

Environmental NGOs ClientEarth, Générations Futures and Notre Affaire à Tous say Groupe SEB should swap harmful chemicals in its products to existing alternatives, such as ceramic coating or cast iron, to limit harm to human health and the environment.

Read more

Croatia’s toxic waste dump scandal shows the cost of Europe’s ‘forever chemicals’

The company uses teflon for non-stick, high-temperature suited coatings of their products.

The substance is one of the ‘PFAS’ polymers, often dubbed forever chemicals, because they break down very slowly, remaining in the environment and human body for a long time. 

PFAS are widely used for food pots, clothes, packaging, and waterproof products.

But since they take so long to decompose, they are often found in soil and groundwater. Many of the substances cause cancer, others are harmful to babies in the womb.

Teflon is allegedly “not absorbed by the human body” and is approved by the World Health Organisation (WHO) for contact with food, the company’s website says.

Read more

Sweden moves to ban ‘forever chemicals’ in consumer products from 2028 as EU-wide ban remains in limbo

However, a recent risk assessment by the EU’s Chemical Agency’s (ECHA), quoted by the NGOs, points out that when overheated or scratched, teflon releases PFAS particles.

It also releases substances harmful to the environment during the manufacturing process, ECHA’s research found in March.

And a new European law on the issue will provide a “more consistent basis for corporate due diligence litigation,” Hélène Duguy, ClientEarth’s lawyer in the case, told EUobserver.

An EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence directive, inspired by French legislation, will oblige all companies based in the EU to address the impact of their operations on the environment and human rights.

Member states must implement national laws fulfilling the obligation by summer 2028.

SEB can show stopping PFAS use is “necessary and feasible,” setting a precedent for others, Dugoy said.

Groupe SEB was approached for comment.

But the Kremlin has said there is nothing to see.]]> First published in Respekt, adapted by EUobserver

Unsavoury news comes from Russia often these days. But the latest unexpected development is the spread of a deadly disease.

Behind the mysterious death of a young woman in Siberia in early October was reportedly pneumonic plague – a disease so contagious it is considered as bad as anthrax, smallpox, and Ebola.

Local authorities in Russia have denied the plague as cause of death, but despite this, they have implemented anti-epidemic measures.

Eva Hrncirova, a spokesperson for the European Commission, said on Thursday (8 October): “Russia should make information about the plague available as soon as possible. This is what we need”.

“We had a meeting with the member states yesterday within the [EU Commission’s] Health Security Committee, and with the WHO [World Health Organization], who are in contact with our delegation in Moscow,” she said.

Russia was asked by the WHO to share “timely, precise, and exact information” about the possible plague in Siberia, she also said.

“We don’t have enough information to assess the epidemiological situation,” she added.

Nothing to see here, says Russia

Pneumonic plague disease can be treated with antibiotics if detected early, but officials beyond Russia’s borders are left with worrying questions.

Did an Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute lab technician in Shelekhov (Siberia) really die of plague?

If so, was it a natural version of the disease, or a more dangerous bacterium modified in military labs?

And what is the risk of the Middle Ages-era disease spreading?

Pneumonic plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis — the same one that once brought devastating plague epidemics known as the Black Death.

The pneumonic form of plague, a disease that killed up to half of Europe’s population in the 14th century, spreads through droplets by coughing or sneezing.

It manifests as severe, rapidly developing pneumonia that almost always ends in death if left untreated. But if antibiotics are administered in time (ideally within 24 hours of the onset of symptoms), the disease is treatable.

Independent Russian-language media say that Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old laboratory technician at the research and hygiene institute in question, accidentally broke a test tube containing plague bacteria in late September, became infected and died in hospital several days later, on 2 October.

Authorities have not confirmed the cause of the woman’s death, letting on only that she died of pneumonia and claiming that no microorganisms connected with her work had been found in her body.

Some 200 of her contacts were subsequently put into quarantine with medical supervision.

Authorities also ordered a three-week quarantine at several hospitals in the wider area, and facemasks for the wider population – even for schoolchildren.

Read more

EU has ‘learned nothing’ from Covid say MEPs, as mpox outbreak grows

Russia’s neighbours, Mongolia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan, have all introduced border controls.

Russia said the epidemic situation in the area was stable, that none of the deceased woman’s contacts had shown signs of infection, and that there was no cause for concern.

However, the head of Russia’s public health authority reportedly travelled to Irkutsk to attend a meeting with local officials, while residents of Shelekhov report that people in protective suits are moving around the town.

And epidemiologists say it is simply not possible that Russia’s public health service would resort to such dramatic measures, including closing hospitals, over a single case of ‘pneumonia of unknown origin’ .

The institute where the laboratory technician worked is said to be a civilian facility that, among other things, researches and monitors the incidence of plague.

In Siberia, especially near the borders with China and Mongolia, the bacteria in question still circulate among animals and occasionally infect humans, as they do in some parts of Africa, where the disease is most common.

    ]]>         Morocco’s surveillance state does not stop at Western Sahara — and Europe can no longer pretend not to know https://euobserver.com/241454/moroccos-surveillance-state-does-not-stop-at-western-sahara-and-europe-can-no-longer-pretend-not-to-know/ Thu, 08 Oct 2026 08:50:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241454 As new evidence emerges of Moroccan spying on Sahrawi activists, including in Europe, European governments continue to deepen their security ties with Rabat without seriously questioning how those capabilities are being used.]]> In April 2021, I told The Guardian that Sahrawi activists were having their phones and internet connections hacked.

    At the time, we could describe what was happening to us. We could not see the machinery behind it.

    Five years later, Amnesty International’s new investigation, “We Start With the Verdict”: Inside Morocco’s Surveillance Machine, gives those warnings a disturbing new context.

    Amnesty describes a surveillance ecosystem involving spyware, physical surveillance, location tracking, informants, judicial pressure and smear campaigns. Western Sahara is not peripheral to its findings.

    The organisation devotes a case study to Sahrawi activists and reports that a former member of Morocco’s domestic intelligence service, identified as “Safir,” described Sahrawis and Riffians as priority intelligence targets, including beyond Morocco. Amnesty says it independently verified his identity, employment and key elements of his testimony.

    The report also contains forensic evidence involving Pegasus spyware and documents cases connected to Sahrawi activism that reached European territory.

    The people Amnesty examined are the tip of the iceberg. They are documented cases: people researchers could interview, devices they could examine, or targets for whom other evidence was available.

    Surveillance is secret by design. Most people never learn that their phones have been compromised, and most suspicious devices will never reach a forensic laboratory.

    That is why the chronology matters.

    Chilling effect

    On 8 April 2021, The Guardian quoted my warning that Sahrawi activists’ “phones and internet connections are hacked.” We were describing the symptoms years before Amnesty’s latest investigation exposed more of the machinery.

    But surveillance is not simply about collecting information.

    When a security service knows who an activist speaks to, where that person travels and what exists inside a phone, information can become power.

    Amnesty documents cases in which private information gathered through surveillance later appeared in media coverage and coordinated smear campaigns against human rights defenders.

    The organisation is careful: it could not independently establish the source of every piece of private material published. But it says the nature of some material raises serious concerns that surveillance-derived information may have reached media actors.

    For Sahrawis, that raises an obvious question: How does private information about activists move from their lives and devices into the public sphere?

    That question deserves independent forensic investigation.

    But Amnesty’s report should provoke another examination — this one in Washington and European capitals.

    For decades, Western governments have built close security relationships with Morocco around counterterrorism, intelligence cooperation, migration and regional stability.

    The question is not whether those relationships should exist. It is whether the West has adequately examined what happens to security capabilities once they are in the hands of its partners.

    Read more

    Sánchez and the EU have decided that Morocco relations are too big to fail

    Amnesty does not establish that every security capability Morocco obtained through Western cooperation was used against Sahrawis. The evidence does not support such a sweeping conclusion.

    It does, however, justify harder questions.

    What safeguards accompanied security cooperation? Who monitored end use? What happens when capabilities developed or acquired in an environment shaped by counterterrorism are directed toward peaceful human rights activism?

    That is the line separating security from repression.

    Western Sahara struggle

    The contradiction is especially striking because Sahrawi human rights activism has often relied on peaceful means: demonstrations, documentation, journalism and engagement with international institutions.

    Amnesty reports restrictions on expression and assembly concerning Sahrawi rights, alongside reports of arbitrary arrests, prolonged surveillance, restrictions affecting families and the dispersal of peaceful demonstrations.

    Europe has encountered similar contradictions in its relationship with Morocco.

    In June 2021, the European Parliament explicitly rejected Morocco’s use of border control and migration, particularly involving unaccompanied minors, as political pressure against Spain.

    Yet the same resolution emphasised the longstanding relationship and cooperation between the European Union and Morocco in counterterrorism, migration and trade.

    That contradiction should matter to Europeans.

    When democratic governments make another state indispensable for stopping terrorism, controlling migration or providing intelligence, they provide more than resources. They provide leverage. Eventually, fear of losing cooperation can make scrutiny of a partner more difficult.

    Europe has confronted another warning sign. In its response to the corruption scandal that engulfed the European Parliament, the Parliament itself denounced alleged attempts by Morocco and Qatar to influence lawmakers and staff through acts of corruption.

    Read more

    MEPs oppose including Morocco in Qatari corruption scandal

    These remain allegations. They do not mean that every European position favourable to Morocco was corrupt. But they demonstrate why foreign influence over democratic institutions requires serious scrutiny.

    European vs American foreign policy

    Western Sahara remains an issue on the United Nations agenda and is tied to a decades-long international process concerning the political future of the territory.

    That should matter to an EU that regularly invokes a rules-based international order.

    Morocco has rejected previous allegations concerning Pegasus and described earlier Amnesty findings as baseless. Amnesty says it provided Moroccan authorities with a summary of its latest findings before publication and invited a response but received none before the report was published.

    Those denials belong on the record.

    So does the evidence.

    The test of a human rights policy is not only how a democracy responds to abuses by its adversaries. The harder test is what it does when credible allegations concern a security partner.

    For Sahrawis, however, this story is older than spyware.

    For nearly half a century, generations of Sahrawis have lived through restrictions and documented abuses connected to political expression over the future of Western Sahara. Children have grown into adults watching what can happen when someone speaks publicly: surveillance, imprisonment, smear campaigns, pressure and fear.

    After all these years, what Sahrawis are asking for is not complicated.

    We are not asking the world to choose an answer for us. Nor should the outcome be written in advance in our favour.

    We are asking for something more elementary: Treat the Sahrawi as a free human being, capable of thinking, choosing and expressing a view about the future of the land he or she calls home without fear.

    It is easy to live in a democratic society, protected by freedom of expression and equality before the law, and then propose a political solution for a distant people who will have to live with its consequences every day.

    But a human question should come before the geopolitical one:

    Would you accept for yourself and your children a political order in which expressing your views about your homeland could expose you to surveillance, intimidation or punishment?

    A Sahrawi is not a number in a diplomatic file, a detail in a geopolitical bargain or a security problem to be managed.

    A Sahrawi is a human being, with a memory, a family, a homeland, an opinion and a future.

    After nearly 50 years, perhaps it is time simply to hear that voice as it is, rather than as others interpret it.

    Give Sahrawis one day without fear.

    One day to speak without surveillance, without pressure and without wondering whether their words will reach their phone, their workplace, their home or their family.

    Do not write the answer for them.

    Just let them speak.

    If any political solution is truly just, why should it fear the voice of the human being who will have to live under it?

That is the wrong question. The real question is not how much the EU budget costs, but how much an insufficient budget will cost us all.  

    Economic benefits of EU membership are estimated to be two to six times the financial contribution of individual member states. For every euro we contribute to the EU budget, we can receive up to six euros in return.

    That is the power of investing together: European investment delivers more than fragmented national spending. And it does so with a budget of just one percent of EU GNI, while national budgets can reach 50 percent.

    The EU budget is not simply money transferred from national capitals to Brussels: it is an investment that creates value benefiting citizens through stronger economies, better infrastructure, food security, cutting-edge research, educational opportunities, regional development, and security.

    Ultimately, all member states benefit from the added value created by the EU, making the concept of ‘net contributors’ obsolete.

    Easing the pressure on national contributions is a legitimate objective, and it has a clear solution: an EU revenue reform.

    The European Parliament supports the basket approach of the European Commission on new own resources and its proposals.     Our position is clear: large global companies that benefit most from Europe’s single market should contribute fairly to the EU budget that makes those benefits possible.

    Cutting the EU budget may look like saving money. But if it means weaker competitiveness, less social investment and a less secure Europe, we save nothing and taxpayers foot the bill.

    Read more

    The European Union’s common budget has not grown in real terms for 40 years. On the contrary, its purchasing power has been steadily eroded due to high inflation. The current EU budget has lost around 10 percent of its purchasing power compared to when it was adopted in 2020. 

    A more ambitious EU budget does not automatically mean that member states will have to contribute substantially more from their national budgets. When amounts are compared in constant prices and as a share of the size of the European economy – like with like – a more realistic picture emerges. 

    In terms of spending capacity, and without counting repayment of the Covid-19 recovery fund (NextGenerationEU), the commission’s proposal for the 2028-2034 budget would be below the relative size of the current 2021-2027 MFF at the time of its adoption.

    Even with parliament’s proposed increase for key EU programmes, member states’ contributions would still not substantially increase. 

    Read more

    Frugal EU states seeking budget cuts are shooting their own regions in the foot

    Let us not forget: Europeans benefit considerably more than their countries’ headline contributions suggest. The single market is the clearest example. By removing barriers between 27 economies, it creates opportunities and delivers growth that no country could generate alone. 

    By reducing the budget, the EU and its member states will have less capacity to deliver the economic and social benefits that citizens expect. We’ll have less cohesion, less competitiveness, a weaker agricultural sector, less global influence, reduced social investment and a much less secure Europe. And this also comes at a cost. A big one.

    Instead of “what can we cut” we should be asking ourselves, “how can we finance a budget that delivers more for all”.  

    If we genuinely want to use limited public resources efficiently, we must invest together. Economies of scale work for successful businesses, and they work for Europe.

      <title>Trump made ‘clear’ that media ban was due to critical coverage, court told</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/oct/08/trump-media-ban-hearing</link>
      <description><p>Lawyer for CNN, MS Now and Politico says Trump admitted he banned networks from White House over their coverage</p><p>Donald Trump continues to be the strongest witness for the media companies arguing that they were unfairly barred from the White House at his direction, a lawyer representing CNN, MS Now and Politico told a federal judge on Thursday afternoon.</p><p>The media coalition was in court asking the judge to extend the temporary restraining order (TRO) he issued on 24 September requiring the White House to lift the ban for 14 days. That temporary reprieve was scheduled to expire on Thursday, but district court judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, said he would extend it until Tuesday and that he would probably rule on a motion for a preliminary injunction by that day. That means the White House will be forced to allow journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico to continue accessing the building until at least Tuesday.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/oct/08/trump-media-ban-hearing">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Millionaire tax no more? Rightwing groups lead effort to repeal Washington state law</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/07/washington-state-millionaire-tax</link>
      <description><p>An initiative on November’s ballot aims to overturn the 9.9% tax on earnings above $1m – who’s winning the fight? </p><p>Voters in Washington state will soon decide the fate of the state’s so-called “<a href="https://senatedemocrats.wa.gov/millionaires-tax-faq/">millionaire tax</a>” – a 9.9% income tax on earnings above $1m that was <a href="https://governor.wa.gov/news/2026/governor-ferguson-signs-millionaires-tax-law">signed</a> into law in March and is now facing a conservative-backed effort to repeal it.</p><p>An <a href="https://leg.wa.gov/media/ucubvqsd/2026-summary-of-initiative-26-645.pdf">initiative</a> on November’s ballot aims to overturn the tax, claiming that the tax represents a slippery slope, and would eventually result in taxes for more than just millionaires. A <a href="https://no645.com/our-coalition/">coalition</a> of advocacy groups and unions opposing the initiative say taxing the state’s 20,000 highest-earning households could raise approximately $3.5bn in necessary annual revenue to fund core priorities like education and healthcare, and expand tax credits and sales tax exemptions.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/07/washington-state-millionaire-tax">Continue reading...</a></description>
