<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comFri, 09 Oct 2026 09:26:12 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[PTSB dissident shareholder Scotchstone latest to signal possible bid]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/09/ptsb-dissident-shareholder-scotchstone-latest-to-signal-possible-bid/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/09/ptsb-dissident-shareholder-scotchstone-latest-to-signal-possible-bid/Fri, 09 Oct 2026 09:26:08 +0000A long-term dissident shareholder in PTSB, Scotchstone Capital, has become the latest party to say it is considering making an offer for the bank, weeks before the High Court is due to hold a sanctioning hearing on its takeover by Austria’s Bawag.

Scotchstone is led by Piotr Skoczylas and had pursued a series of cases in the Irish courts stemming from PTSB’s taxpayer bailout and effective nationalisation in 2011.

“There can be no certainty that any offer will be made or as to the terms on which any offer might be made,” the company said in a statement on Friday.

Skoczylas declined to comment when asked by The Irish Times about investment banking advisers and funding for a potential deal.

The announcement comes seven days after a corporate finance firm cofounded by former Bank of Scotland (Ireland) chief executive Mark Duffy said it is considering a bid for PTSB, almost six months after the bank agreed to sell itself to Austria’s Bawag for €2.97 a share, or €1.62 billion in total.

Has Mark Duffy left it too late to spoil the PTSB party?

Axis Capital, which was set up in Dublin three years ago, said any possible offer would be in cash at a price of €3.20 per share – 7.7 per cent above the agreed price with Bawag.

However, the firm said that it has yet to line up funding for such an offer.

Both Skoczylas and Duffy were open critics of the Bawag deal.

Scotchstone launched proceedings in May in the High Court – which is ultimately overseeing the sale process, structured as a so-called scheme of arrangement – seeking a second vote on the deal by minority shareholders, excluding the Government. The State owns 57.5 per cent of PTSB and voted in favour of the Bawag transaction at an extraordinary general meeting (EGM) in July.

Judge Mark Sanfey said in the May court proceedings that the usual practice is for shareholder voting class composition to be decided at a High Court deal sanctioning hearing. That is due to take place on October 27th.

PTSB secured backing from 91.3 per cent of shareholders – led by the Government – for the Bawag takeover at the July EGM. However, some 36 per cent of minority investors voted against the transaction at the meeting.

PTSB has repeatedly said that it has “very strong” legal advice that only one vote is necessary.

]]><![CDATA[DCC investors to receive a lower extra payment as tech unit sells below target price]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/09/dcc-investors-to-receive-a-lower-extra-payment-as-tech-unit-sells-below-target-price/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/09/dcc-investors-to-receive-a-lower-extra-payment-as-tech-unit-sells-below-target-price/Fri, 09 Oct 2026 09:06:57 +0000DCC Energy shareholders are only set to receive a third of the additional maximum £1.25 (€1.47) payment on offer as part of the group’s takeover deal, contingent on a follow-on sale of it is technology unit.

The Dublin-based group agreed in late July to sell itself to US private equity firms KKR and Energy Capital Partners (ECP) for a £65.25-a-share upfront payment and the prospect of £1.25 extra per share if the Irish company’s tech division achieves at least $800 million (€712.7 million) in a sale.

However, DCC said on Friday that it is set to only receive net proceeds of $701 million for the tech unit, which it has agreed to sell to New York private equity firm One Equity Partners.

DCC said its shareholders are set to receive 42 pence per share from that deal. The technology unit, called Nexora, was already on the market before the consortium make their bid approach in April.

“Under the terms of the transaction agreement [with KKR and ECP], if the technology disposal net proceeds are between $650 million and $800 million, the technology disposal additional consideration will be between zero and 125 pence per DCC Energy share calculated on a linear basis,” DCC said.

That reduces the total value of DCC’s imminent takeover from £5.73 billion to £5.66 billion.

The High Court in Dublin is due to hold a sanctioning meeting on the takeover, which was approved by shareholders last month.

“Nexora has been an important part of the DCC Group for many years and has built a strong market position through the expertise and commitment of its people,” said DCC chief executive Donal Murphy.

“This transaction recognises the quality of the business that the Nexora team has built and, subject to completion, will deliver additional value for DCC Energy shareholders. We believe One Equity Partners is well placed to support Nexora’s continued growth, investment and long-term development, benefiting employees and customers alike.”

DCC, whose businesses once spanned Robert Roberts tea and coffee and waste management, decided in late 2024 to abandon the remaining elements of its conglomerate roots to focus on energy. It subsequently sold its healthcare division and part of its tech business last year, before putting the larger part of the tech unit Nexora on the market.

Murphy signalled in a phone interview with The Irish Times after the shareholder meeting last month that he would like to remain on board to see out DCC’s goal to double the operating profit of the remaining energy division to £830 million between 2022 and 2030.

]]>Nick Bradshaw for The Irish Times<![CDATA[AIB chief Colin Hunt eyes shares worth 100% of salary as bank expected to raise targets]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/financial-services/2026/10/09/hunt-eyes-shares-worth-100-of-salary-as-aib-is-seen-raising-targets-again/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/financial-services/2026/10/09/hunt-eyes-shares-worth-100-of-salary-as-aib-is-seen-raising-targets-again/Fri, 09 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000AIB may nudge its 2026 net interest income forecast higher again in an upcoming trading update, with the expected boost from rising interest rates over the next 12 months lifting its shares, as chief executive Colin Hunt is on track to receive stock this year worth 100 per cent of salary.

The consensus call among analysts is that AIB will post €3.83 billion of net interest income this year, with Denis McGoldrick, an analyst with AIB’s Goodbody unit, estimating it will top €3.85 billion.

AIB projected in July that its net interest income would exceed €3.8 billion this year, up from last year’s €3.75 billion.

On Thursday, McGoldrick also raised his AIB net interest income estimates by 2 per cent for the next two years, which would see it reach €4.21 billion in 2028.

AIB’s shares have risen as much as 23 per cent since it started issuing stock to Hunt and other senior executives in May under a new share awards plan – with no performance conditions attached – to get around a continuing ban on bonuses above €20,000 across Irish banks.

AIB revealed in two filings with the stock exchange, in May and August, that it had issued a total of 75,010 shares to Hunt under the so-called fixed share allowance scheme. The filings were previously unreported by news organisations.

Tax

Childcare

Housing

Social Welfare

Social Welfare

Thank you

In Ireland, we have no line of sight. We’re completely in the dark. The tax windfall could go on for another decade or could fall off a cliff tomorrow. Even the chief financial officers of Apple, Microsoft and Eli Lilly, the State’s three biggest taxpayers, don’t know.

And yet we’re funnelling a huge amount of this windfall (€6 out of every €7) into everyday spending, into income tax breaks, into rent supports, stuff that won’t easily be resiled from.

We’re probably the only State in the world that bases its budgetary arithmetic on a handful of multinationals and the revenues they generate outside Ireland.

“The budgetary arithmetic is constructed on the crucial assumption that corporate profitability continues to expand; any decline in profitability could put a (potentially large) dent in corporate tax revenues,” the Department of Finance said in a report released with Budget 2027 on Tuesday.

If we had saved the windfall element of corporation tax since 2015 – approximately 50 per cent of annual receipts – the State would now have a war chest of €130 billion, capable of generating about €10 billion annually in interest (a typical stock market return).

Government ‘will need to borrow’ for new wealth funds as spending rises at fastest rate in EU, says watchdog

This would be enough to do away with the Universal Social Charge (USC) in one fell swoop, without having to raise tax elsewhere.

The tax-free inheritance threshold of €420,000 and the 33 per cent capital acquisitions tax (CAT) that applies thereafter compares with a pre-crash threshold of €542,000 and CAT of 20 per cent.

Of course Ministers will point to the political straitjackets they find themselves in, the realpolitik of a modern democracy.

If Minister for Finance Simon Harris announced this week that he was planning to save €17 billion of the expected €34 billion in corporate tax this year in the midst of a cost-of-living crisis, he would, like Michael Collins, have been signing his own political death warrant and that of Fine Gael.

And therein lies the problem.

Big change requires a break from the sort of electoral budgeting, the winners and losers narrative, that we’ve had to date. A break from the firefighting, from the sticking plaster measures.

We’re apparently rolling in money, but everyone feels poorer and nobody is happy

We’ve had four years of energy credits and we still have the most expensive electricity prices in the European Union (EU). The credits are not a solution so much as a stop-gap. It’s the same with housing. The more money we spend on the housing assistance payment and other rent supports, the more there is a general erosion in affordability.

One senior figure said that Ireland acts like a poor country, spending money as it gets it, gambling on the back of future revenues, when it is actually a rich country that should be thinking more strategically about its wealth.

“Why don’t we feel the budget day numbers? One reason is that it’s going on hiring more staff across the public sector,” he said.

General government spending jumped by 54 per cent between 2019 and 2025, from €86.9 billion to €133.8 billion, facilitated by record corporate tax receipts.

At the same time, employment in the public sector rose by almost 80,000, from 339,000 to 417,000.

“If the Government thinks this (the additional employment) is warranted, it should be paying for it with money it can depend on,” the senior figure said.

Public spending hits record level as watchdog sharply criticises Budget 2027

The Government seems to have shelved any semblance of a plan to widen the tax base and seems content to play the game with the chips it gets from Corporate America.

Experts disagree on whether Ireland has what’s known in economics as “Dutch Disease” – where a sharp increase in wealth in one sector (usually from the discovery of oil or gas) bids up prices, creating cost challenges and a gradual loss of competitiveness.

The National Competitiveness and Productivity Council says Ireland is now “firmly part of the high-cost cluster in Europe”, with labour costs rising faster than the EU average since 2021. In the three years after the pandemic, labour costs rose faster than in the 13 years previous.

After playing a stellar role in financial crisis, Ireland now sits in an ivory tower at one remove from the financial zeitgeist: debt and fiscal constraint.

Tax receipts more than cover spending, resulting in healthy budget surpluses, while Government debt as a percentage of gross domestic product is now under 35 per cent. In the UK (in 2025) the equivalent was 101 per cent. In France, it was 115 per cent. In the US, 121 per cent.

There’s a good chance we’ll come to regret this period as a missed opportunity.

]]><![CDATA[Is the State’s new investment account going to be a good deal?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/08/is-the-states-new-investment-account-going-to-be-a-good-deal/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/08/is-the-states-new-investment-account-going-to-be-a-good-deal/Thu, 08 Oct 2026 12:12:00 +0000Is the State’s new investment account going to be a good deal? The announcement of key details in the budget has certainly attracted renewed public interest. But it is essential to understand the fundamentals of the scheme to judge how it might fit in to your personal financial plan. And in assessing this, investors need to realise that they are going to be largely on their own.

Most of those providing the plans – the big banks and insurance companies initially – are likely to follow a low-charge model, meaning they will not offer personalised advice. Instead people will get some online essentials about the various plans on offer and choose – via a bank app, for example – what level of risk they wish to take.

It will, of course, be open to potential investors to seek personalised guidance from an adviser, or sign up for a more bespoke scheme, but this will cost more. All kinds of funds offered by brokers will be “wrapped” in the new scheme, in other words constructed to take advantage of it.

But charges here will be higher. As the offers develop, options are likely to grow. But cheap and cheerful will be the hallmark of the initial approach when the big players kick it off next July.

The tax-free nature of the scheme on holdings up to €50,000 is attractive. But still, there are some steps to assessing whether taking part works for you.

The first key point is that the return has to be greater than that available on a risk-free asset such as a bank account. Many people have cash currently in demand accounts with the main banks offering very low returns. But they could get 2 to 3 per cent – or even a bit more – if prepared to move into a savings account which might require notice on withdrawals.

Lower-than-expected annual €12,000 investment account limits may curb take-up

Returns are subject to deposit interest retention tax (Dirt) at 33 per cent, so that needs to be deducted – a third of your interest goes to the taxman.

Traditionally, stock markets have offered significantly higher returns than this. The Stoxx Europe 600 index, for example – the kind of index which an investment under the scheme might be based on – has had an average return of 8 per cent over the past 20 years. Most European indices has returned at least 6 per cent over that period.

But the Stoxx index lost 12 per cent in 2022, as inflation surged following Russia’s full scale invasion of Ukraine. So the first thing for new investors to understand is that you have to be able to ride out the bad years and let the averages – the fact that equities tend to go up more years than they go down – lead to gains over time.

Of course we cannot be sure that stock markets will behave in future like they did in the past. And we don’t know what markets will look like next July when the funds are launched, but this will need to be taken into account.

A bursting of the artificial intelligence (AI) bubble or the wider knock on to bond markets from rising interest rates present risks.

Investors will have a broader exposure than those who put cash into Eircom when it floated in 1999, but its initial rise and then fall as tech shares were hit as the dot.com bubble burst is worth noting, nonetheless.

If investors are happy to lock in their money for a period, then history suggests that equity market will beat deposits. Their next key call will be how much risk to take. At least initially, funds are likely to be marketed as high, medium and low risk. The latter will put some cash in traditionally less volatile areas such as bonds (though these have been on a volatile run of late).

This is where the lack of advice on basic products could be difficult for new investors in choosing where to put their money. We will have to see how the offers line up, but the funds will make more sense for those willing to take a somewhat higher level of risk and thus get a higher return over time. You need to beat the bank account return and also take into account the costs of the scheme.

The key cost most investors will need to factor in is whatever the provider is charging to offer the service. The indications are that there will be an effort to keep costs on basic offers down below 0.5 per cent – but remember this is a charge on the total value of the fund. There are also likely to be products offer bespoke advice but with higher charges, likely more than 1 per cent.

A charge of 0.5 per cent would be €100 on a €20,000 pot, while 1 per cent would be €200. This may not sound like a big difference. But over time charges matter as more money is taken out of the pot and there is a cumulative hit. Over 10 years the difference between a 0.5 per cent fee and a 1 per cent one on a €50,000 pot would be well in the thousands of euro.

The best hope for investors is that the big banks and their investment arms will keep the charges low to try to hold on to money which people are moving from deposits with the same group. But charging structures will be vital to assess. And these low-cost products leave investors making their own decisions.

The next bar to jump is the State tax. A big attraction of the scheme is that normal taxes on investment – capital gains tax and the taxes paid on exchange-traded funds – will not apply. It is only on pots of more than €50,000 where the new 1 per cent charge on the balance above this figure applies. So a couple could have two accounts summing to €100,000 and pay no tax.

Like charges from the provider, the 1 per cent will be significant for bigger investors. If an investor has saved, say, €100,000 then the annual charge will be €500 (1 per cent of €50,000).

As with charges, this eats away at the pot over time. And – crucially – this will be charged in good years and in bad – in other words in years when the value of your investment falls you will still pay the 1 per cent charge on balances of more than €100,000.

In Sweden this type of levy was initially charged on the whole sum saved and this led some experts to conclude that the tax advantage offered by the products – which like Ireland spared investors from capital gains tax – was limited.

The key attraction, they said, was simplicity, the fact that the provider does all the administration and also avoiding having to pay a big capital-gains bill all at once when the investment was sold.

More recently Sweden also introduced a tax-free scheme this year, which means a pot of up to €27,000 will not face a levy. The tax on amounts above this is 1.065 per cent.

For Ireland, investors will need to realise that the sums change significantly when savings become subject to the 1 per cent charge. There will probably still be tax advantages, but they will be narrower on the part of the fund exceeding €50,000 – and having to pay no matter how the fund performs is significant in bad years.

The bottom line is that the new investment vehicle is better suited to slightly riskier investments which offer a higher potential return. It also requires the investor to understand the risks and the need to be able to leave money where it is – if necessary – to recover from bad years. And to understand the impact of the 1 per cent charge on larger sums and the fees on all investments.

For many it may still offer an attractive part of a wider savings plan, which might also include a pension plan, some highly tax-incentivised additional voluntary contributions and some money in the bank for the “rainy day” when funds might be needed quickly.

But understanding what is and what is not on offer is vital. Just because this is a “State” scheme does not mean any kind of guarantee is on offer. It is not a special savings incentive account Mark 2. As the radio ads say. investments can fall as well as rise.

Budget Q&A: Submit your questions to our expert panel on budget day

The Minister said the measure would save parents €2,220 annually per child, a significant saving from after-tax income.

Not for the first time, there appears to be a substantial “reality gap” between the Government’s understanding of the “maximum” cost of care and the real maximum under its own core funding rules.

The amount childcare providers can charge is divided into bands based on the hours of care provided. The Minister’s figures are based on Band E, covering children in care for between 40 and 50 hours a week.

The issue is that most parents – certainly in and around Dublin – are paying under Band F, for children in care for 50 or more hours, which is significantly more expensive.

And how does that explain the difference between €959 and €1,400 a month?

The €1,400 figure is the full gross cost before you deduct the subsidy parents are entitled to under the National Childcare Scheme. Once you apply the subsidy, the figure falls to €959. Some parents may just be looking at the top line of their childcare bill.

In a devastating analysis, John Mearsheimer of the University of Chicago describes the war on Iran as “the mother of all strategic blunders”.

Among other things, he says, the United States went into the war on the false claim that Iran was on the verge of acquiring a nuclear weapon; Washington thought air power alone would produce regime change, which has never worked; it had no contingency plan for dealing with Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

The stupidity is indeed impressive. Even now we cannot guess how it ends. Yet there is a counterargument. The war may indeed be a strategic blunder. But the economic damage has been surprisingly modest.

As Johannes Urpelainen of the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies said in August, “Many experts initially thought that this supply disruption would send oil prices to USD 200 per barrel, causing massive inflation and a global recession. Urpelainen says that: “First, the energy transition has reduced the global economy’s dependence on oil. Second, supply chains have proven resilient and adaptive. Third, producers outside the Middle East have acted fast to produce more oil and natural gas. Finally, drawdowns of global oil inventories have filled the remaining gap.”

Flexibility is notably true of the Gulf. As former diplomat Mohammed Elsoukkary writes: “By the end of September preliminary estimates placed regional crude exports at approximately 16.3 million barrels per day, compared with 19.5 million in February, including roughly 9.7 million moving through Hormuz.”

Nevertheless, the disruption to oil supply, oil prices and the world economy more broadly has, in truth, been quite surprisingly manageable. In terms of the overall economy, this is, as Nouriel Roubini says in Project Syndicate, in large part due to the investment boom triggered by artificial intelligence (AI).

But, for the future health of the world economy, it is not the level of investment, but its rate of growth, that matters, as does the ultimate economic contribution of AI itself. Surely at some point investment will slow. As to the economic contribution of AI (or indeed its doomsday properties), who knows with confidence?

There exist other sources of fragility. One, which I discussed previously, is the manageability of global debt at a time of rising interest rates. France, the United Kingdom and US are in the crosshairs. There is a particular risk for countries whose public debt is overwhelmingly short-term since, as a result, they enjoy little insurance against the impact of higher inflation on interest rates.

Seeing it laid out in such a stark manner was sobering.

The programme initially focuses on presenter Gráinne Seoige’s own experience of having a deepfake image created of her while she was campaigning in the general election in 2024. Two years on, the distress it caused was evident.

But things got worse. With the help of Ceartas, a tech company that started as a free service to tackle so-called revenge porn, she found out the real extent of the problem. A visibly upset Seoige was told that they had uncovered more content, images she hadn’t known about.

There were stories from others who had been similarly affected – model and presenter Maria McGuigan, poet Noel Fleming and an unnamed 15-year-old girl – each one horrifying in its own way.

The message was clear: this isn’t an isolated issue, and it isn’t going away any time soon.

By the end of the year, nudification apps are expected to be banned in the EU. But it has taken far too long to get to this point.

Nudification apps were thrust into the spotlight in January, when images of mainly women and sometimes underage subjects that had been digitally undressed by xAI’s Grok chatbot were published on social media platform X.

If you needed any other reason to remove yourself from the platform, the company’s response – first ignore it, then make access to the image-editing feature available only to paying subscribers – might have pushed you over the edge. Eventually, X cut off Grok’s ability to alter images of real people in places where it breached the law, but only after heavy pressure from authorities. The move came too late for women – and children – who had been affected by the incident, and is not a watertight solution to the problem.

Data Protection Commission investigates X over ‘nudification’ of images via Grok

While the Grok incident may have highlighted just how easy it is to fake such images, it wasn’t the first to do it, nor was it the worst offender. It was just the most visible. I used an AI image editor to change an innocuous photo of me, fully clothed at a sports event, into one where I was posing in a skimpy bikini. The software refused to do anything more extreme than that, but it is enough. The image editor was a free tool that surfaced in a quick Google search; imagine what you could find if you were willing to spend time to hunt down the most lax software out there. Another few clicks brought me to an AI girlfriend creator and a NSFW (not safe for work) image generator.

This is just scratching the surface of the issue. As the analogy goes, if you see two ants in your home, you don’t have a two-ant problem. Somewhere there is a nest, and until you deal with that, you will continue to have problems.

The difficulty here is that it is almost impossible to root out the nest. While the EU may ban nudification apps and Irish law can take action against those who share nonconsensual explicit images, it cannot stamp out the technology behind it. Apps can be – and are – removed from app stores to make them less visible. But as we already know, things can live on in the quieter corners of the internet, just out of sight but still accessible. As AI skills grow, AI models can and are being modified by users to fit their needs.

Unless there is a concerted global effort to deal with the issue, the apps and those behind them will simply move out of the law’s reach.

That is assuming the ban is passed without being watered down or challenged in some way. In Minnesota, where similar action on such software has been almost unanimously backed by politicians, the proposed law is currently on hold after xAI brought a legal action against it, claiming it imposes an “overbroad, content-based ban on free speech and the tools of visual expression”.

An AI company, owned by a billionaire, claims that a law that bans apps and websites using AI to create nonconsensual sexualised images and videos of people infringed free-speech rights. Even where the political will is there to do it, there are challenges to overcome.

Female-looking AI agents were paid less than male ones in virtual office, study finds

Who asked for this? Why do we need it? The AI companies that have enabled this, intentionally or not, need to take a long, hard look at themselves in the mirror. I once asked an executive in a tech company why, given the obvious potential for abuse, the company was developing tools to generate increasingly realistic images.

The answer? Because the company’s competitors would do it.

The one weapon we have to fight back is education. The idea that the image is fake so it doesn’t have an impact or any legal repercussions is being eradicated by programmes aimed at educating children. Perhaps we should focus on adults, too. Make “I didn’t know” an invalid defence against creating the images.

And while we are at it, erase “we didn’t mean it” from the tech companies’ book of excuses.

Capital acquisitions tax (CAT), sometimes referred to as gift or inheritance tax, is a beneficiary tax. It’s payable whenever a beneficiary receives a gift or inheritance that exceeds their tax-free threshold amount.

What determines the level of CAT is the relationship between the beneficiary and the person making the gift or inheritance, says solicitor Matthew Johnston, managing partner at Nooney & Dowdall Solicitors in Mullingar.

When a beneficiary receives a gift or inheritance, they can fall into one of three different tax-free threshold groups, depending on their relationship to the person giving the gift, says Johnston.

A child falls into the Group A threshold and can now inherit up to €420,000 tax free from a parent, a €20,000 increase announced as part of Budget 2027.

A nephew or niece falls into the Group B threshold of close blood relatives, which also includes siblings, a grandparent, aunt and uncle. They can now receive a maximum gift or inheritance of €44,000 tax free from each other due to a change in this week’s budget.

Do I still owe tax if my mother’s house sold for less than expected?

Cousins, close friends, neighbours, carers or others all fall into a Group C threshold. The most they can receive tax free is now €22,000.

There is also the small gift exemption to consider. Anyone is entitled to give €3,000 per calendar year tax free to someone else. If a gift is more than €3,000, the first €3,000 is tax-exempt and the balance is deducted from the lifetime tax-free threshold they have in relation to the person giving the money.

With all of this in mind, it would be wise for the aunts and uncles here to give their nephew the €10,000 by way of four gifts of €2,500 each, says Johnston.

This way, the individual gifts fall below the allowable €3,000 small gift exemption.

“There will be absolutely no tax consequences for the nephew if they do that,” says Johnston.

It also means that, should any of his individual aunts or uncles want to give him a more substantial sum in future, their nephew’s €44,000 Group B tax-free threshold remains intact and can be availed of.

“You are preserving the entirety of the nephew’s lifetime tax-free threshold from his aunts and uncles,” says Johnston.

Be sure to give the €10,000 as four individual gifts, he advises.

“If the aunts and uncles give it to one sibling and he transfers it to the nephew, it might look like that uncle gave the entire sum, rather than €2,500 coming from each individual,” says Johnston. “Get the nephew’s Iban and do four separate transfers.”

This could be a simple email to their nephew from each aunt and uncle, explaining that the money is a gift, he says.

Trying to make sense of it all, Political Editor Pat Leahy writes in our lead story this morning that the Government “unveiled an €8.5 billion budget package on Tuesday to bring public spending to a record level, and drew sharp criticism from the State’s budgetary watchdog for increasing the reliance on ‘high-risk corporation tax’.

“The package will bring public spending to €125.6 billion next year despite tensions in Government over the insistence of Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers to limit spending growth to 6 per cent next year.”

If you want to check what is in the budget here is our detailed list of the Budget 2027 main points.

And here are some of the details on the €1.3 billion income tax package.

  • Level at which workers enter 40 per cent income tax rate increased from the current €44,000 for a single person to €46,500

The Irish Times view: Coalition being driven by events

What’s our view on the budget? Well, you can find it here.

Given the international upheavals this is understandable, to an extent. But continuing to base a public finance strategy on the health of a half dozen multinationals does not look wise.”

Opinion: Somewhat muted reaction from all sides to budget

The first budget of the Simon Harris-Jack Chambers combination, and the second of this Coalition, was presented on Tuesday to a somewhat muted reaction from all sides, writes Political Editor Pat Leahy.

Virtually all its main features had been flagged in advance and there were no last-minute surprises to excite supporters or inflame opponents; surprises, after all, can be risky and this Government is highly risk-averse.

The budget speeches were mostly received in polite silence. Government supporters were appreciative, but hardly ecstatic; Opposition TDs were critical but not exactly brimming with righteous fury. The responses flooding into the inboxes of TDs and journalists from the army of interest groups were mostly of the “we welcome ... but not enough was done” variety.

If a budget is an opportunity for a government to provide a statement of what it is about, then this Government is about keeping things going as they are, making incremental improvements, and above all, not annoying anyone.

Reaction to Budget 2027

Government TDs around Leinster House were largely pleased with the budget package, though the reaction elsewhere was mixed.

Many representative and interest groups welcomed aspects of the budget but said that it did not go far enough.

Owen Reidy, general secretary of the Irish Congress of Trade Unions, said the budget was “a halfhearted apology for last year’s”.

“The Government has taken some bare minimum measures, but it is far from the workers’ budget the Government claimed, and does not make up the ground workers have lost,” he said.

Employers’ group Ibec welcomed aspects of the budget but said it was disappointed the Government had accepted recommendations to increase the national minimum wage.

Bid to cut smoking ‘abject failure’, Dáil told

A packet of 20 cigarettes will cost €20.15 following a €1 increase in the budget, bringing the tax take to €16.03 or almost 80 per cent of the retail price, writes Parliamentary Correspondent Marie O’Halloran.

Ireland continues to have the most expensive cigarettes in Europe and now has the second highest cigarette prices in the world behind Australia, where a 20-pack costs €21.02.

The €1 increase was accepted in the Dáil on Tuesday night by 110 votes to 48.

The pro-rata increase in the price of a typical pouch of roll-your-own tobacco is €1.39, bringing the retail cost to €29.72.

Introducing the tax, Minister for Further and Higher Education James Lawless said the increase on tobacco products would yield approximately €63.1 million in a full year, and €5.1 million for the remainder of 2026.

Bakhurst rejects assertion that pace of RTÉ reform is too slow

RTÉ director-general Kevin Bakhurst has rejected Minister for Communications Patrick O’Donovan’s assertion that the pace of reform at Montrose has been inadequate after the Government cut the national broadcaster’s funding in Budget 2027, business reporter Ian Curran writes.

RTÉ reached a landmark multi-year funding deal with the previous government in 2024. Under the agreement, the broadcaster would receive €725 million over three years: €225 million in 2025, €240 million in 2026, and €260 million in 2027.

However, O’Donovan announced today that RTÉ will receive €240 million next year, saying that he was not happy with the pace of change at the broadcaster and its transition to being a “more agile, smaller” organisation.

The decision appears to have been made at the last minute, catching the broadcaster off guard, according to Bakhurst. He told staff in an email on Wednesday that the he “completely rejects” the assertion that the pace of reform has been too slow.

Bakhurst said that the decision “is one we had not anticipated and will inevitably impact our ability to deliver our five-year strategy”.

Over the past two years, RTÉ has axed its in-house documentary unit, outsourced its religious affairs programming, and cancelled Upfront with Katie Hannon. It has also set out plans to outsource Fair City and The Late Late Show.

However, the Coalition has reportedly been disappointed by the pace of a job-shedding programme, through which RTÉ aimed to shed around 400 jobs.

“I think it is well documented that you know that there were issues with regard to the voluntary redundancy that could be achieved in the last round, and obviously we would hope that that would be able to be advanced,” O’Donovan said today.

Speaking at a press conference, the minister also said that his department had “very little scope, in relation to what resources we had available”.

McDonald says budget was ‘devoid of imagination and ambition’

Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald said Budget 2027 was the 11th from Fianna Fáil-Fine Gael and “I have listened to a different version of the same budget 11 times now”, Marie O’Halloran reports from the Dáil.

McDonald said the Coalition parties “always put those at the top first, the golden circles ahead of the ordinary workers and families of Ireland, the people who actually create the wealth”.

The Government has “billions and billions” with “record surpluses”, but she asked: “Is this the best they could do?”

She reiterated it was a “gone-before-you-get-it budget, devoid of imagination and ambition, so disconnected, the product of an inability to listen or to understand what workers and families are going through”.

“There is nothing here that says solutions. Instead, people got half measures, tinkering at the edges or nothing at all.”

She said two weeks ago the Tánaiste told people “help is on the way” but she asked what help, saying “there is no dedicated cost-of-living package” while more than 300,000 households could not pay their electricity bills.

“A million households are on the hook for further energy price hikes, and nothing to help them pay their bills. We asked the Ministers to provide the €400 energy credit. They could not find the money for it, they say, but they did find the money find for generous tax breaks for their pals in high places, the developers, landlords and bankers, all the usual suspects.”

She added: “There is no sign of a windfall tax to hit the bumper profits of the big energy companies, which squeeze every euro they can from their customers. They let them off scot-free and did not put a glove on them.”

Culture Minister says it’s his job to ‘step on toes’

Minister for Culture Patrick O’Donovan has said it is his job “step on toes” to stand up for the sectors he is responsible for during budget negotiations, Political Correspondent Jack Horgan-Hones writes.

Speaking at his post-budget press conference today, the Limerick County TD also confirmed there is no funding allocation yet made for major sporting events such as the NFL which the government may seek to host in the coming period - with funding only made available for contractually agreed events like the European football championship and the Ryder Cup.

After a budget process which reportedly saw tense and difficult discussions between O’Donovan and Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers, the culture minister said:

“I have a job to do for the arts, culture, communications media and sports community in Ireland, given the seal of office that the President gave me to carry out my constitutional prerogatives, and if that means I have to step on toes to stand up for the people who I am the minister with responsibility for … that is my job. "

He said he had a “very good” relationship with Chambers and defended his budget allocation, but also suggested he was constrained in what he could allocate to RTÉ due to the sum that was agreed.

He rejected suggestions he had walked out of budget negotiations. “When a meeting ends, people naturally go about the rest of their lives,” he said, defending the budget he agreed as “very significant”.

Culture card for teens might happen in future, says O’Donovan

O’Donovan did not confirm whether a pre-paid €100 culture card for 16-year-olds would be rolled out before the end of next year, as he had suggested before the budget - but which was latterly ruled out by Chambers.

“If we want children to come off of their phones … it’s a very small sum of money for 16 and 17-year-olds, government has to put to be prepared to put their hands in their pocket to do that,” he said.

“The concept of the culture card is not in any way going to stopped ... There obviously will be things we would have loved to have done this year but we’ll get around to doing them next year and the year after.”

He said he would not make progress on Programme for Government commitments if he accepted every “hump and bump in the road” as the end of a proposal.

Nature groups criticise lack of budget funding

A dedicated Government fund to save Ireland’s nature will be announced soon, Minister of State Christopher O’Sullivan has said, Climate and Science Correspondent Caroline O’Doherty reports.

Minister rules out raising cap on Help-to-Buy scheme

Screen Producers Ireland ‘significantly concerned’ by budget

Budget 2027 will create a “very challenging environment” for the Irish film and television industry, screen producers have warned, after the Government cut RTÉ’s funding and decided against increasing TG4’s and Screen Ireland’s allocations, Ian Curran reports.

Government committed to increasing Defence Forces personnel – McEntee

Minister for Defence Helen McEntee has said increases in Defence Forces spending show “very clearly” the Government is committed to increasing overall spending and “increasing numbers”, Vivienne Clarke reports.

Means test for carer’s allowance to be eliminated in Government’s lifetime – Calleary

Minister for Social Protection Dara Calleary has said the Government will “get rid of” the means test for the carer’s allowance during the lifetime of this Government, but it has to be done on a “sustainable basis”, Vivienne Clarke reports.

The fuel allowance will be paid over 28 weeks this winter, he added.

Budget 2027 ‘anything but a workers’ budget’ – ICTU

The general secretary of the Irish Congress of Trade Unions has described Budget 2027 as “anything but a workers’ budget”, Vivienne Clarke reports.

The budget had made the ongoing dispute even more difficult to resolve, he told RTÉ Radio’s Morning Ireland.

‘People have never felt as poor’ – Mairéad Farrell

Sinn Féin’s spokeswoman on public expenditure, Mairéad Farrell, has said there could have been a fairer way in Budget 2027 for the Government to address the challenges facing workers, Vivienne Clarke reports.

“This State has never been as rich, but people have never felt as poor as they do today.

‘We’re trying to protect people’: Taoiseach defends budget

Taoiseach Micheál Martin has defended Budget 2027, saying the Government was trying to protect people “as best we can in the midst of an international crisis”, Vivienne Clarke reports.

Martin said the budget came amid “major international global uncertainty” – oil and energy crises – which is fuelling inflation.

“We’re trying to protect people as best we can in the midst of that international crisis by tax measures for the workers, by a really strong focus on disability over the last two years, and in terms of the childcare costs on families, and reducing those significantly.

“Those three pillars were probably the major beneficiaries of the budget,” he said.

Martin said the “fundamental driver” for putting money aside was demographics, noting Ireland will have “far more older people” in the future, who will be more dependent on social protection and health.

“We will have to provide for that into the future,” he said.

The Taoiseach acknowledged there needed to be a change in focus in the taxation framework, in the composition of revenue coming into the exchequer.

“We have to change focus in our taxation framework to encouraging indigenous enterprise and scaling up enterprise, and that’s why the seed capital gains tax has been reduced somewhat, and why I think we have to do far more to create our own indigenous base, to kind of create a greater balance,” he told Newstalk’s Claire Byrne Show.

“We need to think more about how we scale our own companies, and how we ensure that they have capital available to them to grow and to develop.”

Budget struck a ‘balance’, McEntee says in response to Ifac criticism

Minister for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee has responded to criticism by the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council (Ifac) of overspending, and over-reliance on corporation tax, by saying the budget has got the balance right, Political Correspondent Harry McGee reports.

“People are saying we’ve spent too much. There’s people who said we haven’t spent enough. So I think what we try to do is get a balance here,” said McEntee.

She said that spending growth would be maintained at 6 per cent.

Arguing that the spending was an investment in people’s futures, she said it was being put into service, into retrofitting homes, investing in SMEs, and also supports for people feeling the impact of energy price hikes.

The Fine Gael Minister was one of a large number of Fine Gael TDs and Ministers who handed out the party’s pamphlet on Budget 2027 to Luas commuters at Stephen’s Green on Wednesday morning.

Pressed about the criticism by Ifac she said the Government had done its own figures as well, and the teams in the two Government departments responsible for the budget had set out a trajectory that she said was manageable.

McEntee said the Government was putting an additional €1 billion into the two fiscal buffer funds, on top of the planned €5 billion for 2027.

Asked if Minister for Culture Patrick O’Donovan was the biggest loser of the budget, given that the €100 culture card did not materialise, McEntee said every department had seen an increase.

It takes a giveaway budget of €8.5bn to not annoy anyone – except Patrick O’Donovan

She also said Chambers was very clear yesterday when saying that the card project, which is part of the programme for government, is still being worked on.

“It wasn’t achieved in this budget but we have three more budgets,” she said.

Asked if O’Donovan was naive in flagging it in advance, she said the commitment from Government was there and that all Ministers wanted to achieve as much as they could in their own departments.

‘A joke’: Pensioner criticises €3 increase to living alone allowance

Tánaiste and Minister for Finance Simon Harris and Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers have been taking live questions on RTÉ Radio’s Today with David McCullagh from those affected by the budget.

One 80-year-old caller, Noel, is critical of successive governments, saying he and his wife “worked all our lives, paid our taxes”.

Eight years ago, his wife died, he says, adding: “Our government’s reaction was to half my household income,” going down to €243 at the time.

“You could survive on that for a week or two but for it to be a permanent, it’s not just cruel, it’s just not fair.”

Told by McCullagh of the increase of €3 to the living alone allowance, Noel responds: “Please don’t go there.”

“That in itself is a joke. If my lovely wife had survived, she would be receiving €330 a week so the Government are saving that.”

He adds he would love to “meet the genius” behind the €3 increase.

Chambers acknowledges many like Noel are under “significant pressure”.

“Over a two or three year period, we didn’t see an increase in the living alone allowance and we have increased it at a similar level to what we increased it three or four years ago,” he says, adding that it represents a 14 per cent increase.

“I accept, if you look at it in isolation in a single week, it obviously isn’t what many people would expect,” he says, adding however that the full year value will be €1,300 in 2027.

It will also coincide with increases in core welfare rates, including the pension, alongside an increase to the fuel allowance.

Noel tells Chambers not to mention the increase in the fuel allowance, saying it is not an increase.

Noting that the term has effectively been reduced after an extension last year, Noel says the Government “actually reduced the fuel allowance by €32”.

Chambers says that was an “exceptional” extension, adding that the €5 increase is permanent.

Another caller, Megan, says the €550 monthly childcare fee cap is welcome, but it will not come into effect until September 2027 and will only apply to providers in the National Childcare Scheme.

She and her wife have a son aged just over six months, and they have been unable to get a place in such a creche as he is not eligible yet due to his age. Providers are also “heavily oversubscribed”, she says.

She estimates they will be paying €1,450 per month for a childminder once they are both back at work full time.

She asks what the Government will do for families in her situation.

Harris says the increase to the childminder benefit was an effort to make it more attractive to be a childminder. Under the change, childminders will be able to earn €20,000 before paying tax.

Chambers adds that work was ongoing on wider reforms around “making sure those outside of the National Childcare Scheme are included within it”.

Harris says he believes vapes are the “revenge of the tobacco industry”.

The Tánaiste says the HSE “absolutely does not recommend vapes” for those who wish to stop smoking, and instead recommends nicotine patches, gum, lozenges and patches.

He consulted the Department of Health on the issue, he says, adding there is a public health concern around vapes.

He says the Government “has to raise revenue”, noting that a packet of cigarettes has also been increased by €1.

“We’re particularly concerned about vape usage for our young people,” he says.

‘A KitKat budget from a TikTok Tánaiste’ - Bacik

Consequences of Middle East war to ‘reverberate for some time’ - Taoiseach

Taoiseach Micheál Martin has started off a Budget 2027 debate of more than seven hours in the Dáil today, Marie O’Halloran reports.

He said to build a greener and more sustainable economy “this transition has to be managed in a fair and balanced way”.

The Government had invested €1.5 billion into ESB “to boost capacity and our renewable energy infrastructure”.

“And it is why we will transfer €2 billion to EirGrid over the coming years to invest in the resilience of our energy grid," he said.

He said it was a budget that supports households and businesses to reduce exposure to future energy shocks.

The doctor says: “Go see the Tánaiste and Finance Minister Simon Harris orating in the Dáil. The country is flaithiúlach because of the Yanks. He’s throwing money around. Great celebrations will be had. It will surely cheer you up.”

The man bursts into tears: “But doctor, I am Tánaiste and Finance Minister Simon Harris.”

It’s budget day in Dáil Éireann, the day when the Government makes us all do sums. We’re rolling in money these days (apparently) but everyone also feels poorer (evidently) and nobody is happy (clearly).

Harris looks miserable. Though that’s probably because he’s been up all weekend with a new baby, not the budget! His wife Caoimhe gave birth to their third child over the weekend.

Barbara and Frank Chambers are in the distinguished visitors’ gallery observing the work of their own baby, Jack Chambers, the Minister for Public Expenditure. I believe they were up all night with him too.

Anyway, at 12 o’clock, out come the best boys from behind the bike shed of Government Buildings, professional budget models Chambers and Harris, holding up their big colourdy budget books, opening them up to reveal mysterious charts and doing some synchronised waving at the behest of the snappers. (“Finally!” they say, “a photo of men in suits.”)

Ah, we love the symbolic theatre of it all. Chambers wears a salmon pink tie. Harris a blue one. Once upon a time, people took bets on the Minister for Finance’s tie colour on budget day. It’s clear to conspiratorial types that the colour choices are signalling coded messages to their masters in the bond markets.

An hour later, Harris takes to his feet in the Dáil. He recently brought back an old Fine Gael greatest hit favouring people who “get up early” and this budget, he tells us, is for hard-working people. He presents his budget as an attempt to manage the cost-of-living crisis. He talks for some time.

Then he figuratively high fives Jack Chambers into the fray to name-drop Seán Lemass twice and champion the cause for fiscal responsibility (the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council keen audibly from somewhere beyond the chamber). He talks for some time.

The gist of budget day is that the Government lists all of the things that are right with the country (unemployment rates, budget surpluses, tax cuts) with the numbers that support that.

And then the opposition spokespeople list all of the things that are wrong with the country, using the numbers that support that (housing issues, homelessness, child poverty, poor disability services).

The short version is that the Government are focused on future global volatility. The opposition are more focused on the failures of the present.

Sinn Féin’s Pearse Doherty kicks off the Hour of Hate. He quickly segues from the shortcomings of the budget (he dubs it the “Gone Before You Get It” budget) into a more general assessment of the missteps of Government when it comes to the number of children in poverty and the number of people who are homeless.

He targets a lot of his ire at Taoiseach Micheál Martin, which is a little insulting to Harris and Chambers on their big day. The Taoiseach rolls his eyes and shakes his head and looks appalled with the impertinence of it all. Harris mutters and Chambers stares into the middle distance, thinking no doubt of his days budget-modelling in the forecourt.

It’s enough to make a man start smoking, really. Sadly, they have added a euro to the cost of a packet of fags.

The other spokespeople follow the same theme.

There are lists of shortages and service failures. The gist of the opposition critique is that this is not a progressive budget targeted at those who are suffering. Instead, they say, it is one that largely benefits wealthier voters, tinkering with the higher rate of income tax which a majority of Irish workers do not pay and offering untargeted measures to alleviate cost-of-living pressures. It has enough references to risk-takers to trigger those with collectivist tendencies.

People Before Profit-Solidarity TD Richard Boyd Barrett angrily tells the people of Ireland to “get their placards ready”.

Socialist Party TD Ruth Coppinger accuses Chambers of going “full Musk”, setting up “Doge” with his newly announced public spending efficiency taskforce – a reference to the Tesla boss’s Department of Government Efficiency that took an axe to US government spending.

Labour’s Ged Nash says it’s not a budget for “those who get up in the morning” but one “for those who can afford a bloody good lie-in”. (I think people in the entertainment industry call this “a callback”).

On both sides of the house, there’s a sense that it’s very important to make the most of our current budget surpluses, given the state of the world. There is, after all, no way of knowing what the exchequer receipts will look like in the future.

But TDs differ significantly on what it means to make the most of it. There is also only so much talk of millions and billions that a person can take before their eyes glaze over and it begins to feel like Monopoly money.

But it’s real money. And everyone is very aware that the Monopoly board might someday be yanked off the table.

A couple with a combined salary of €100,000 will be better off by €1,382. Additional supports via rent credits, childcare and energy will also boost income.

Budget Q&A: Submit your questions to our expert panel on budget day

So the Government is doing more than merely inflation-proofing the budget against wage growth. But it can’t shield households from inflation in the wider economy. Utility and grocery bills are set to accelerate in the coming months while fuel (petrol, diesel, home heating oil) has already spiked.

The Government can’t chase this cost-of-living squeeze as much of it stems from wider geopolitical events. And to chase it, in an economy already running up against capacity constraints such as full employment, will only result in more inflation.

The long-awaited savings scheme

Since being appointed Minister for Finance last year, Simon Harris has championed the idea of a State savings scheme to unlock the €170 billion sitting in deposit accounts here.

Budget 2027 main points: €10 increase in pension and welfare rates; 20 cent per ml tax on vapes

The new Savings and Investment Account, announced as part of Budget 2027, incentivises ordinary people to invest by offering them an investment scheme with a tax-free threshold of €50,000 and a flat tax of 1 per cent on the value of the account thereafter.

There is a maximum contribution limit of €12,000 annually.

The Government appears to have gone for a more restricted version of the schemes seen in other countries, perhaps under pressure from banks which are making a tidy profit from holding the €170 billion on deposit with the European Central Bank (ECB) while paying minimal rates of interest here.

The UK’s counterpart scheme is tax-free with an annual contribution cap of £20,000 (€23,600), while the Swedish equivalent has a flat tax above a certain threshold but no annual contribution cap.

The Government, which examined both those schemes, seems to have adopted a cautious approach, one that is unlikely to change the retail investment culture here. “For a lot of taxpayers, in the long term, it will probably be more tax efficient to maximise tax relief arising on pension contributions before contributing to an investment account set up after July 2027,” said Robert Dever, head of tax at Eversheds Sutherland.

Minimum wage increased but living wage deferred

The Government has agreed to a recommendation by the Low Pay Commission for a further 79 cent increase in the minimum wage, which will bring the current rate from €14.15 per hour to €14.94. But there is speculation that it may have deferred the introduction of a living wage, which was due to replace the minimum statutory rate in 2029, with businesses complaining of cost pressures.

Last year, Minister for Enterprise Peter Burke announced a three-year delay to the introduction of the living wage (a higher rate of pay that covers basic living costs), pushing the target date out from 2026 to 2029. This may have been moved again as the Government tries to placate the business lobby. The Department of Public Enterprise are due to release details on Wednesday

Budget 2027: big business pays the bills as Coalition rolls the dice

The minimum wage has become a big flashpoint, with worker advocates demanding relief from the high cost of living and business groups warning of severe labour cost pressures.

Government’s fiscal discipline faces testing times

Being cash rich in a world characterised by excessive Government debt comes with moral hazard. The State’s record corporate tax receipts have run in parallel with a worrying build-up in spending. General government spending has jumped by 54 per cent since 2019, from €86.9 billion to €133.8 billion last year.

According to the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council, net spending, which includes tax changes, has increased by an average of 10 per cent over the last four years, which is double the rate of increase that the Department of Finance deems sustainable.

Budget Calculator 2027: Here’s how this year’s budget will affect your income

Judging from the fractious negotiations in the lead-up to Budget 2027, Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers appears to be trying to halt this expenditure creep. In current spending terms, this budget allows for an annual increase of 6 per cent, but spending overruns have become routine and what’s announced on budget day has a habit of being revised up.

Proposed €100 culture card 16-year-olds bites the dust

One of the novelty kites flown in recent weeks was the idea of a culture card for 16-year-olds. Minister for Culture Patrick O’Donovan floated the idea of giving teenagers a one-off voucher to spend on arts, cultural and music venues, an idea that seemed to have the support of Harris.

However, the move appears to have been slapped down by Chambers amid reports of a testy encounter between the two Ministers. One version has it that O’Donovan walked out of the meeting after being told his department’s budget allocation was already too high. The €100 voucher would have cost €8 million.

]]>Nick Bradshaw / The Irish Times

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3444253/">
   <title>Ukraine will Verkehr in Kiew absichern</title>
   <description>Die ukrainische Hauptstadt Kiew steht derzeit in besonderem Fokus umfassender russischer Angriffe. Raketen und Drohnen schlagen den ganzen Tag über ein, es gibt immer wieder Tote und Verletzte. Ein neues russisches Angriffsziel sind die Verkehrsbrücken über den Dnipro. Moskau will das öffentliche Leben in der Ukraine zunehmend unerträglich machen und die Menschen zur Flucht zwingen. Kiew reagiert mit verschiedenen Schutzkonzepten – wie effektiv diese sind, ist noch ungewiss.</description>

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3444460/">
   <title>Zu warmes Meer heizt „El Nino“ weiter an</title>
   <description>Die für das Wetterphänomen „El Nino“ entscheidende Meeresregion ist aktuell so warm wie noch nie seit Beginn der Aufzeichnungen. Laut Daten der Plattform „Climate Reanalyzer“ der University of Maine in den USA hat die durchschnittliche Meeresoberflächentemperatur in der „Nino 3.4“-Region mit Stand 5. Oktober erstmals die 30-Grad-Marke erreicht, wie am Donnerstag bekanntgegeben wurde. Damit liegt die Wassertemperatur 3,39 Grad über dem Durchschnitt des Referenzzeitraums von 1991 bis 2020. Experten sind besorgt, denn das zu warme Meer heizt „El Nino“ weiter an.</description>

An overwhelming majority of MPs in the Sejm, the lower house of Poland’s parliament, have voted in favour of a bill that would introduce tough new anti-alcohol measures, including a ban on all forms of advertising and on sales in shops during nighttime hours.

The legislation must still pass through the upper-house Senate and will then require the signature of President Karol Nawrocki. However, given the level of support – with only two small far-right groups voting against the bill – it appears likely the measures will be approved.

#PILNE | Sejm uchwalił ustawę wprowadzającą na terenie całego kraju nocną prohibicję, zakazującą reklamy alkoholu i podnoszącą opłatę za sprzedaż alkoholu. https://t.co/OawNUdtqM6

— tvn24 (@tvn24) October 8, 2026

The new restrictions were initially proposed in separate bills submitted by two junior members of Poland’s ruling coalition, The Left (Lewica) and the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), which were combined into a single package.

The measures include a ban on the sale of alcohol for off-premises consumption between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m., with local authorities able to extend those hours up to 9 p.m. to 9 a.m. if they wish. Bars, clubs and restaurants would still be allowed to sell alcohol for on-premises consumption as presently.

Almost 200 Polish municipalities, including large cities such as Warsaw and Kraków, have already introduced their own local bans on nighttime alcohol sales.

In the first six months following the implementation of its restrictions in 2023, Kraków saw a nearly 50% decrease in nighttime police interventions, with other cities reporting similar improvements.

 

The newly approved bill also includes a complete ban on advertising and promoting alcoholic drinks. Those who violate the prohibition can be fined up to 1 million zloty (€228,400).

Packaging for alcoholic drinks will be required to include warnings about their harmful effect on pregnant women and minors. The legislation also toughens requirements for shop staff to check the age of buyers if they suspect they may be underage.

The cost of licences to sell alcohol will be increased from 525 to 1,050 zloty for drinks with up to 18% alcohol content and from 2,100 to 4,200 zloty for stronger drinks.

Warsaw has announced a ban on nighttime sales of alcohol in shops.

The new measure will come into force on 1 June 2026 and will apply from 10 p.m to 6 a.m. across the entire city https://t.co/A7xVvJMpvU

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 12, 2026

In a vote on Thursday night, the bill won support from 400 of the 433 MPs present in the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament. The only groups that did not vote in favour were the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP).

The legislation now passes to the upper-house Senate, which can suggest amendments but only delay, not block, a bill’s passage. Once finally approved by parliament, it will reach the desk of President Karol Nawrocki, who can sign the bill, veto it, or send it to the constitutional court for assessment.

Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has vetoed a record number of bills. However, given the level of support for the alcohol bill in the Sejm, including from the largest opposition groups, Law and Justice (PiS) and Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), it appears likely he will sign it.

Poles are eating more meat but drinking less alcohol, continuing a long-term trend, new data show.

The average person in Poland ate 82kg of meat last year, up 7.5% from 2024 and 22.7% since 2005.

They also drank 82 litres of beer, down 18.7% since 2018 https://t.co/FxFMupWLRv

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 1, 2026

In June, an IBRiS poll for the Rzeczpospolita daily found that 55% of Poles support some form of ban on nighttime alcohol sales while 43% are opposed. A survey by IBP for Super Express published today showed even stronger support, with 67% in favour of a ban and only 26% opposed.

Recent data released by Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, showed that alcohol consumption among Poles is continuing its recent decline.

In 2025, the average Pole drank 81.7 litres of beer, down 4.9% from the previous year and 18.7% from the peak of 100.5 litres per person in 2018. Likewise, consumption of spirits and liqueurs fell 5.9% year-on-year in 2025 to 3.2 litres per person. That was 13.5% down from a peak of 3.7 litres in 2019.

However, alcohol consumption is still higher than it was two decades ago, with the average Pole drinking 28% more spirits and 1.2% more beer in 2025 than in 2005.

]]> Polish man suspected of helping Russian plot to assassinate Zelensky sentenced to 5.5 years https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/08/polish-man-suspected-of-helping-russian-plot-to-assassinate-zelensky-sentenced-to-5-5-years/ Thu, 08 Oct 2026 15:58:23 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105244

A Polish man has been sentenced to five and a half years in prison for spying on behalf of Russia. The tasks assigned to him included reconnaissance of Rzeszów-Jasionka airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky while he travelled through Poland.

The sentence was handed down by the court of appeal in Lublin on Thursday, increasing by two years a jail term issued by a lower court earlier this year. The ruling is now final and binding.

Sąd zaostrzył karę dla Pawła K. Chodzi o współpracę z rosyjskim wywiadem #lublin #szpieg #rosja #wywiad #wyrok https://t.co/Vg2zTx35l4

— Fakt (@Fakt_pl) October 8, 2026

The 51-year-old former Polish soldier, who has been named only as Paweł K. under privacy law, was detained by Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) in April 2024.

Investigators found that the suspect had declared his willingness to collaborate with Russian intelligence and, between December 2022 and March 2024, had established contact via email and instant messaging with Russians involved in military operations against Ukraine, including army officers.

Prosecutors determined that Paweł K. had been assigned tasks including gathering and transmitting information regarding security at Rzeszów airport, which is the main hub for goods and people being transported in and out of Ukraine.

“These activities could have been used by Russian intelligence services, including in the context of planning a possible assassination attempt on the head of a foreign state, that is, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky,” wrote Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office earlier this year.

Poland and Ukraine have revealed further details of a foiled plan to assassinate @ZelenskyyUa at Poland's Rzeszów airport.

A Polish man was last month indicted in relation to the incident, which he is accused of seeking to carry out on behalf of Russia https://t.co/Lrp99vH4s2

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 23, 2025

Last year, the head of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) said that Paweł K. had been “recruited decades ago and firmly believed in the Soviet cause”. Polish prosecutors have not commented on that claim.

However, they did find that the suspect had declared his willingness to join Russian “sabotage structures”, including the Wagner mercenary group and Unit 29155 of the GRU, Russia’s military intelligence agency, which is tasked with carrying out destabilisation activities.

Paweł G. denied the accusations against him and claimed that he had actually been trying to help capture Russian war criminals by deceiving them into trusting him, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP).

His defence attorney argued that the information Paweł G. had transmitted regarding Rzeszów airport was “trivial and publicly available”, according to news website Onet.

 

In January this year, Paweł K. was found guilty of espionage and illegal possession of ammunition by the district court in the city of Zamość, which sentenced him to three and a half years in prison.

However, prosecutors appealed against that ruling, arguing that the suspect deserved a longer jail term of seven and a half years. In a judgement issued on Thursday, the Lublin appeals court agreed that Paweł G’s initial sentence had been “grossly lenient” and increased it by two years, reports PAP.

“Submitting an offer to work for…the intelligence service of a country that is at war with a country directly neighboring Poland, a country that is making quite extensive unfriendly gestures towards Poland, cannot be treated leniently,” said judge Artur Achrymowicz.

Poland has charged three of its own citizens with working on behalf of Russian intelligence.

They are accused of spreading disinformation, conducting reconnaissance of NATO troops, and undergoing firearms training in preparation for acts of sabotage https://t.co/maYd0kb9HW

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 20, 2026

Poland has become a primary target for acts of espionage, sabotage and disinformation conducted by operatives working on behalf of Russia.

In many cases, they are so-called “disposable agents”: individuals already on the ground, often amateurs hired and paid through messaging apps such as Telegram, rather than professional spies or soldiers.

The AWB last year launched 48 investigations related to espionage, more than twice as many as in 2024. Over those two years, there were more espionage investigations than over the previous three decades combined

A report published earlier this year by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism found that Poland is the “primary focus” of Russia’s sabotage operations in Europe.

Poland is the "primary focus" of Russia's sabotage campaign in Europe, finds a new report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism.

Among 151 incidents identified since 2022, 31 of them took place in Poland – more than in any other country https://t.co/QXfSI00FD6

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 3, 2026

In January, Polish prosecutors indicted five people – four Ukrainian citizens and one Russian – accused of carrying out a plot on behalf of Russia to plant explosives in packages that were then dispatched by courier services across Europe.

In April, prosecutors charged a soldier from Poland’s Territorial Defence Force with seeking to spy on behalf of Russia. The following month, three Polish citizens were charged with working on behalf of Russian intelligence to spread disinformation and conduct reconnaissance of NATO troops.

In July this year, a Russian married couple who had been studying in Poland were jailed for spying on behalf of Moscow and involvement in a plot to send a parcel bomb.

A sign installed to warn the public about damage caused by beavers has been destroyed by the beavers themselves, according to the Polish foresters who erected it.

The incident was reported in a post on social media by the forestry district of Lubliniec in southern Poland, which shared photos of the sign, which read “Warning! Damage caused by beavers”. The wooden post it was displayed on had been destroyed in an apparent beaver attack.

“We wanted to warn you about the potential consequences of beaver activity at the pond and the surrounding area – since beavers dig burrows under the road and fell trees near the pond – but the beavers didn’t want you to be warned, so…they cut down the oak post displaying the hazard notice,” wrote the foresters.

“So, if you are around the pond, please exercise caution; and if you spot a piece of wood sticking out of the ground that has been gnawed by beavers, just imagine there was a sign there reading ‘Warning! Damage caused by beavers’.”

Beavers were once almost hunted to extinction in Poland. By 1928, it was estimated that only 235 remained in the country. However, thanks to postwar efforts to reintroduce the animals into the Polish wilderness, the beaver population has grown and is currently estimated at around 150,000.

Ecologists note that beavers play an important role in tackling drought by retaining water through the dams they build. Those dams also create “oases of biodiversity”, notes the state water agency PGW WP.

However, the rodents can cause damage to roads, houses and farmland, which has led some to call for culls to keep beaver numbers down.

One person has been killed in a knife attack on a primary school carried out today by a 15-year-old former pupil. It comes just a day after another knife attack by a 19-year-old on a different school in Poland, which left eight people injured. The assailant was also carrying a homemade explosive device that failed to detonate.

Meanwhile, police also announced today the arrest of a 17-year-old who had reportedly threatened to attack a school and was found to be in possession of knives.

The developments have caused shock in Poland, a country where such violent incidents are normally rare. “We are seeing a radicalisation of young people,” warns the education minister, who has called for tougher controls on online content.

W rękach Policji jest już 15-latek, który około godziny 9 wszedł do szkoły w miejscowości Leszczydół-Nowiny, w powiecie wyszkowskim i ostrym narzędziem ranił 3 pracowników placówki. Wśród rannych jest dyrektor, który ujął 15-latka. Policja była na miejscu już po kilku minutach od… pic.twitter.com/EV1RPP7LA5

— Policja Mazowsze (@PolicjaMazowsze) October 8, 2026

The latest attack took place in a primary school in the village of Leszczydół-Nowiny, around 60 km (37 miles) northeast of Warsaw, on Thursday morning.

A 15-year-old former pupil of the school entered the facility and stabbed three members of staff, including the principal, who managed to subdue him. One of the victims, a 37-year-old female caretaker, died from her injuries. The other victim, a teacher, was hospitalised.

The attacker was detained and will appear before a family court, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily.

 

The incident comes just a day after another similar tragedy only 50 km away, in the town of Ostrołęka. On Wednesday morning, a 19-year-old attacked a vocational high school, leaving four students, two teachers and two bystanders injured before being captured.

The assailant, who has been named only as Jakub Z. under Polish privacy law, is a student at the school. On Wednesday evening, national prosecutor Dariusz Korneluk told broadcaster TVN that the attacker had a homemade explosive in his backpack “that almost detonated”.

“The backpack was already in the computer room and, only due to the responsible actions of the teacher and the students, was it thrown out of the window” after smoke had begun to billow out of it, he said.

Justice minister Waldemar Żurek pledged that “prosecutors will ensure that the perpetrator answers for every blow inflicted and faces the legal consequences…There is no tolerance for violence in Polish schools”.

The Warsaw region, which includes Poland’s capital and its suburbs, had the highest employment rate in the European Union last year, according to new Eurostat data.

The employment rate among people aged 20-64 in the region stood at 86.9%, more than 10 percentage points above the figure for the EU as a whole. It was also the highest recorded for Warsaw since data began to be collected in 2013.

Last year, only four EU regions had employment rates of at least 85%. Warsaw was followed by Prague in the Czech Republic at 86%, Finland’s Åland Islands at 85.5%, and Utrecht in the Netherlands at 85.4%.

The EU average stood at 76.1%, slightly below the target of 78% the bloc set for itself for 2030.

At the other end of the scale, 64 of the EU’s 244 regions had employment rates below 74% last year. The lowest was recorded in France’s overseas departments of Mayotte (36.9%) and French Guiana (50%), followed by Italy’s Calabria (50.3%), Campania (50.8%) and Sicily (51.4%).

After Warsaw, the second-highest employment rate in Poland was recorded in the central Łódź province (80.8%) while the lowest was in the southeastern Subcarpathian province (73.2%). The figure for the country as a whole was 78.8%, which was only the 13th highest in the EU.

In addition to topping the overall employment rate ranking, Warsaw also had the third lowest rate of youth employment (for people aged 15-29) at 3.9%, higher only than Yugozapaden in Bulgaria (3.8%) and Zeeland in the Netherlands (3.6%).

And it had the third-highest rate of employment among people with tertiary education (93.5%), behind only Portugal’s Região Autónoma dos Açores (94.6%) and Yugozapaden (93.6%).

At the same time, job creation is slowing, while some industries – including manufacturing, automotive, furniture and construction materials – are coming under pressure, according to experts.

Earlier this year, Poland’s airspace was violated by a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile, which landed in a field. On one night last year, around 20 Russian drones crossed the country’s eastern borders, and last month a Russian military helicopter briefly entered Polish airspace from Kaliningrad.
