Solutions like this, where a collaboration can measurably accelerate not only a founder’s path, but also time to market for our customers, are core to our investment strategy.”

The move comes as Teradyne has been increasingly investing in AI across its ecosystem. In its most recent earnings statement, the North Reading, Mass.-based company marked its fifth consecutive quarter of growth.

Teradyne credited AI as a main driver of its revenue growth. In addition, Universal Robots, a Teradyne subsidiary, recently released its seventh-generation cobot arm, which is designed to take advantage of AI advances.

“The investment will support Bright Machines’ continued growth and the expansion of its AI infrastructure manufacturing platform, including the engineering and deployment work behind the collaboration, integrating Teradyne’s robotics and test technologies with our platform, and bringing that combined architecture to customer sites,” Fiaz Mohamed, chief growth officer at Bright Machines, told The Robot Report. 

Teradyne and Bright Machines jointly automate production

The partners said they plan to integrate Teradyne’s technologies into Bright Machines’ production environments. This will include precision robotic assembly, robotic loading and unloading of test equipment, and autonomous movement of materials.

“Teradyne brings industry-leading capabilities in test and robotics that complement Bright Machines’ software and automation platform,” Mohamed said. “Integrating those systems with our platform will connect robotics and test data with assembly, inspection and product-genealogy data, giving customers confidence in a pre-tested manufacturing platform that can improve with every system built at the scale they need.”

The companies hope to deploy the technology at Bright Machines’ and customer sites. At these sites, the Bright Machines manufacturing platform, Universal Robots’ force- and power-limited robots, and Teradyne’s board test systems would operate together on a production floor. Each produces a distinct stream of information: assembly and inspection data, robot and material-movement data, and electrical test results.

Teradyne said connecting these data streams with Bright Machines’ product genealogy  and manufacturing capabilities will create an end-to-end system. This system links design decisions, assembly execution, and electrical performance. 

“We’ve already begun adding Universal Robots to our lines, and the teams have begun identifying and developing areas for technical integration across test, robotics and automation,” Mohamed said. “We expect this to be a phased effort tied to specific manufacturing applications and customer requirements, and we aren’t announcing a timeline for a fully integrated system today.”

“What limits automation today is not what a robot can physically do but how much engineering it takes to tell it what to do,” said James Davidson, chief AI officer at Teradyne. “When a robot can pick up a new task in hours instead of being re-engineered over weeks, high-mix, short lifecycle production becomes the default. Once build data and test data sit in the same loop, the line can correct itself quickly.”

Teradyne noted that AI infrastructure is demanding. Product complexity is high, design cycles are short, quality requirements are stringent, and schedules leave little room for rework.

Manufacturers serving this market increasingly value an integrated approach spanning manufacturing design, intelligent robotics, autonomous material handling, quality assurance, and end-to-end production intelligence, delivered as one coordinated system.

“The next generation of AI infrastructure calls for a manufacturing approach that is more automated, software-defined, data-driven, and responsive to change,” said Sviat Dulianinov, CEO of Bright Machines. “Teradyne’s expertise, and the investment that comes with it, helps us validate that approach. Their robotics and test technologies are complementary to our platform, and together we can help customers simplify integration, accelerate deployment, and maintain a complete production data thread.”

Partners share AI infrastructure experience

AI infrastructure is driving one of the largest electronics manufacturing buildouts in recent history, noted Teradyne. As hyperscalers, AI laboratories, silicon providers, and OEMs invest in next-generation compute, manufacturing has become a determinant of deployment speed, quality, and economic value, it added. Manufacturers place a premium on lines that can be reconfigured in software as product designs refresh.

Teradyne claimed that it is working with manufacturers across that ecosystem, including electronics manufacturing services (EMS) and original design manufacturer (ODM) providers, OEMs, and hyperscalers. It said it supplies robotics and test technologies to make high-mix, high-value electronics production possible.

Burlingame, Calif.-based Bright Machines brings a software-defined manufacturing platform spanning design, robotics, automation, inspection, material movement, production intelligence, and operations. The company has deployed more than 130 microfactories across over 10 countries and active AI infrastructure production in the U.S.

“AI infrastructure combines complex products, short design cycles, and demanding quality requirements, with very little room for rework,” Mohamed said. “Clean, unified data is the key to manufacturing quality AI infrastructure at scale, but production data has traditionally been siloed across stations, lines, and sites. In our work with Teradyne, connecting design, assembly, inspection, material movement and electrical testing in one system creates a continuous data thread, allowing manufacturers to identify problems earlier, respond faster, and understand exactly how every unit was built and tested.”

A Unitree humanoid robot at the China Humanoid Robot Conference in Seoul in March.

Robots are back in the national spotlight, and this time, the conversation is about more than what they can do. It’s about who controls them and what data they collect.

The restrictions on foreign-produced robots by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) underscore the growing scrutiny of these machines as connected infrastructure. As robots take on more work in factories, warehouses, and other high-stakes environments, questions about how they use data and make decisions are becoming harder to ignore.

That scrutiny is likely to accelerate the move toward on-premises AI architectures and smaller, specialized models that can run closer to where robots operate. The more control companies want over who can access a robot and its data, the more incentive they have to keep sensitive processing close to the machine.

Companies deploying physical AI today need to decide which AI workloads belong on the robot, what can remain in the cloud, and whether the underlying technology stack can meet rising expectations for security, safety, and supply-chain transparency.

Robot security is becoming an architecture question

In July, the FCC added foreign-produced advanced robotic devices to a list of technologies it deems to pose unacceptable national security or safety risks. That designation prevents new devices from receiving the FCC authorization generally required to be imported, marketed, or sold in the U.S.

The restrictions apply broadly to advanced mobile robots, including humanoids and quadrupeds, that can collect detailed information about the environments around them. Officials have warned that foreign-made robots could give foreign actors a way to conduct surveillance, collect sensitive data, or remotely interfere with machines operating inside American facilities.

But hardware origin is only one part of the security equation. If a robot is continuously collecting information about a facility and sending it to an external cloud service for processing, companies also have to consider where that data goes and who can access it.

Editor’s Note: The Robot Report is hosting a free webinar on October 27 called “The FCC Robotics Ruling: What Automation Buyers Need to Know.” Join leaders from Vecna Robotics, Locus Robotics and the Association for Advancing Automation (A3) for a discussion about what the FCC action means for the robotics industry and the organizations investing in automation.

Moving intelligence closer to the robot

Keeping more inference on the robot or inside a facility was already attractive because it improves latency and reliability. The recent regulatory change could make local processing a higher priority for a broader range of AI workloads, especially those involving internal operational data.

For core control functions such as motion control and safety monitoring, local processing is non-negotiable. The bigger change is likely to happen higher in the stack, where robots interpret instructions, analyze their surroundings, respond to anomalies, and make task-level decisions.

Those workloads can be computationally intensive, and the cloud offers more processing power than most edge hardware. But relying on external cloud resources can introduce network dependence and require operational data to leave the facility. Companies will likely need to run more of that intelligence locally within tighter compute limits.

Why SLMs could gain ground

The more organizations move higher-level intelligence on-device, the less practical it becomes to rely on cloud-dependent large language models (LLMs) for every task. That strengthens the case for small language models (SLMs) designed for industrial environments.

A robot operating in a defined environment doesn’t always need a model built to handle almost any question. It needs one that understands the context of the facility and can perform the tasks required there reliably.

That doesn’t mean the robot has to be locked into a single job. With the right context and access to local data, an SLM can support a wider range of applications within the same facility. For example, a robotic arm working on one production line could be moved elsewhere in the factory and adapted to perform a similar task in a different production environment.

SLMs can be fine-tuned on a factory’s own data and run directly on edge hardware with lower compute requirements than larger general-purpose models. For many industrial use cases, the combination of specialization and flexibility across changing local deployments can make them a stronger fit for the job.

More local control means more integration work

These changes raise the bar for system design at U.S. companies building or integrating robots. You must ensure that controllers, sensors, safety systems, and AI hardware can work together reliably and that the full system can be secured and maintained over time.

When you buy a finished robot, many integration and certification decisions have already been made. Building one from components puts more of the engineering burden on your organization: How will components be integrated? How will safety be validated? How will firmware be maintained, and where will critical parts come from?

The right suppliers can help answer those questions with tested components, traceable sourcing, and deployment support.

U.S. businesses need suppliers that can show how their components have been tested together, document where critical parts come from, and provide the safety and governance support needed after deployment. When those pieces have already been validated to work together, builders can spend less time solving component-level integration problems and more time focusing on the complete system.

Building for control from the start

The most immediate effect of the FCC action is on sourcing. Its longer-term impact may be even bigger: architecture.

As robots move deeper into sensitive and mission-critical environments, companies will have to evaluate them on more than capability or performance. They need to know whether critical processing can stay local, where robot data is going, and how much confidence they can place in the underlying components.

Businesses that build those controls in from the start will be better positioned to deploy physical AI without creating problems they have to unwind later.

Robotics and artificial intelligence are deeply intertwined technologies. Where the former serves as the “body,” the latter provides the “brain,” with organizations continuing to develop the technology from traditionally rigid machinery into smart, adaptive agents designed to enhance productivity and operational efficiency. In particular, the evolving sector of physical security can benefit from the advancements in physical AI of the past few years.

In 2026 alone, over $23 billion has been invested in organizations focused on improving how the two technologies work together. Much of the focus is on how developments can apply to protecting people and property.

With more complex risks and threats against critical industry infrastructure such as data centers and manufacturing plants, organizations face new challenges in protecting these assets. Physical security challenges arise from connectivity

Understanding the primary challenges in 2026 can highlight where physical AI and robotics can fit into an organization’s physical security strategy. Almost all leading risks and threats fit into the broader categories of cyber-physical convergence, legacy constraints and global volatility.

As cybersecurity and physical protection increasingly intersect, organizations face new threats. Connected security systems can include interlinked cameras, access control and sensors that, if malicious actors attacked the central platform, could leave considerable vulnerabilities, opening assets up to theft, damage, and disruption. 

One example of the impact is last year’s Jaguar Land Rover incident. Stolen credentials and social engineering from allegedly state-sponsored actors gained access to the automaker’s IT infrastructure, causing a major disruption. It completely halted physical production, costing the British economy an estimated $2.5 billion.

The incident demonstrated how legacy technologies and volatility are leading to a growing number of cyber and physical security risks. Operating older hardware and software only enables personnel to react to events rather than attempt to prevent them, which cannot suffice in a security environment that becomes more vulnerable with growing tensions in both the geopolitical and socioeconomic spheres.

Real-world applications for physical security

The rapid development of physical AI in the field of robotics is only hastening the deployment of assets for security purposes. They are already active in various hospitals, shopping malls, and education campuses across the world.

]]> Ecosia’s decision to drop French AI provider Mistral is not a move towards Chinese technology, but rather a shift towards more affordable, energy-efficient open AI models, founder and CEO Christian Kroll clarified in a conversation with EU-Startups.

“We’ll probably be using Melious.ai in future. Unlike Mistral, this is a European company that offers high-quality, affordable AI inference powered by green electricity,” shared Christian in an exclusive interview.

The Berlin-based search engine recently made headlines after POLITICO reported that it was replacing Mistral with open models, including Chinese offerings such as Alibaba’s Qwen, Z.ai’s GLM and Moonshot AI’s Kimi.

However, Christian stressed that the company’s focus is on open models rather than their country of origin. These offer lower costs, greater flexibility and reduced energy consumption, aligning with Ecosia’s environmental mission.

Addressing concerns about political censorship in Chinese AI models, Christian explained that Ecosia can switch to alternative models when dealing with sensitive subjects, such as questions about Taiwan. The company is also working to eliminate political biases from its AI-generated answers.

The models are accessed through German platform Melious, which operates on European infrastructure powered by low-carbon energy. This allows Ecosia to use internationally developed AI while keeping its infrastructure and data processing in Europe.

Christian also reiterated his concerns about Mistral’s European sovereignty, arguing that its reliance on foreign investors, particularly from the United States, undermines its independence.

This follows a period of significant expansion for Paris-based Mistral AI. In September 2026, the company secured €3 billion in Series D funding, led by Samsung Electronics, at a valuation exceeding €21 billion. The investment followed €722 million in debt financing announced in March to develop its first large-scale data centre near Paris, as well as a €1.7 billion Series C led by Dutch semiconductor equipment manufacturer ASML in September 2025.

Its latest funding round included US investors such as Andreessen Horowitz, Nvidia and Salesforce Ventures, alongside European backers including ASML and Bpifrance. Mistral also participated in a €2.9 million investment in Italian infrastructure startup Clastix.

These come amid wider investment in European AI infrastructure, with financing announcements covered by EU-Startups in 2026 totalling approximately €6.2 billion, including Mistral’s own funding.

Christian contrasted this with Ecosia’s own funding history. The company grew largely without external financing, receiving early backing from German entrepreneur Tim Schumacher. In 2018, Ecosia adopted a steward-ownership structure that prevents the company from being sold or distributing profits to shareholders.

For Ecosia, the switch reflects a broader vision for European technology: rather than depending on individual AI developers, European companies can build competitive, independent services using open models running on European infrastructure.

For Mistral, however, this development implies a loss of trust in what is considered one of Europe’s most promising AI companies.

]]> Klarent (formerly fore ai), a Zurich-based autonomous software testing startup, has closed a €7.13 million Seed funding round.

The round was led by London-based Mosaic Ventures, with participation from Moonfire Ventures and a number of prominent angel investors, including Jürgen Galler, a former Director at Google, Harris Barton, and AngelInvest Ventures, among others.

“With AI, code generation is scaling faster than our ability to test it, so QA will become the key bottleneck. Asheem and Momo saw this at Google before most of the industry did. What convinced us was their insistence on determinism – using AI to write tests, not to run them – which is why enterprises are trusting Klarent in production. We’re delighted to back the team as they expand to the US,” said Chandar Lal, Partner, Mosaic Ventures.

The startup was founded in 2023 by two ex-Google engineers, Asheem Panakkat, who serves as CEO, and Momchil Ivanov, who serves as CTO. Panikkar spent more than a decade at Google leading teams on Shopping and Lens, while Ivanov worked as a Staff Software Engineer focused on information retrieval. Together, they spotted how the explosion in code being written as large language models became more capable meant the systems used to verify that code were nowhere near ready to keep up.

Their solution: deterministic autonomy. Instead of leaning on large language models to run tests directly, Klarent’s agents use LLMs only to author test code. Once written, the test code executes in a deterministic, repeatable manner, combining the adaptability of AI with the rigour expected in production engineering. There is also a human-in-the-loop verification layer on top, ensuring customers pay only for verified outcomes. 

“At Google, Momo and I could see two things coming at once: LLMs were getting better fast, and the amount of software being created was about to explode. The question that wouldn’t leave us was the feedback loop. How do you keep these coding agents honest? We began by building evals for LLMs and quickly realised the bigger opportunity was QA itself. As AI writes more of the world’s code, testing stops being a cost centre and becomes the thing that determines whether any of that code can be trusted,” said Panakkat.

Their approach has already won over enterprise clients across Europe. JD Sports, Swiss media group NZZ, and mobility company Sixt all use the platform. At JD Sports, Klarent’s AI agents automate multi-system workflows across the e-commerce pipeline, an automation that the retailer said its own teams could not replicate.

The funding will be used by Klarent to support its entry into the United States, building on the momentum seen with its European enterprise customers. The company also plans to grow its engineering team and broaden its cross-platform testing capabilities across web and mobile. It is also pushing into financial services, working with banks and insurance firms where the cost of a broken software release can be catastrophically high.

]]> Besso, a Bern-based startup that helps companies manage the complexity of international trade regulations, has secured €4.29 million (CHF 4 million) in funding.

The funding came from a single large European family office, which opted to remain anonymous. This is a departure from traditional early-stage funding rounds, which have multiple backers, and the company says the funding raised from a single long-term investor was deliberate. 

“We have always been very deliberate about building Besso around real customer demand rather than funding milestones. The traction we are seeing now tells us that the time is right to invest more aggressively in growth. Having one long-term investor take the entire round gives us both the resources and the focus to do exactly that,” said Philip Sieber-Gasser, founder and CEO of Besso.

Founded and headquartered in Bern, Switzerland, Besso helps multinational corporations turn the growing complexity of international trade regulation into a source of competitive advantage. It has built an AI platform that continuously monitors over 1,250 trade regulations and tariff schedules across global corridors, automatically identifying where companies are overpaying on duties and offering them opportunities to recover costs through preferential tariff rates and free trade agreement (FTA) eligibility.

According to the company, global tariff teams miss out on preferential tariff rates on around 30% of eligible shipments. This reportedly costs mid-size importers between $2 million and $15 million annually. In addition to cost, these trade teams are also grappling with more than 7,000 regulatory changes every week across major trade corridors, a figure that has grown due to geopolitics and tariff volatility.

Besso’s AI platform replaces the manual, error-prone processes reliant on spreadsheets, PDFs, and consultancy dependency that most companies currently use to manage their requirements. Besso has already built a strong roster of global clients, including Danone, Unilever, AB-InBev, BASF, Coca-Cola, Heineken, Philip Morris International and Syngenta. The company says additional Fortune 500 companies recently joined the platform.

Alongside its strong client base, the company has built a team with expertise in legal research and is supported by academic partners including the Geneva Graduate Institute, the World Trade Institute, and ETH Zurich. Its advisory board includes Jean-Daniel Gerber, a former Swiss Secretary of State for Economic Affairs, along with other leading trade law academics and AI specialists.

The company, a Venture Leaders alumnus, plans to use the funding to increase its headcount, scale capacity to serve a rapidly growing multinational customer base, and advance its technology platform through continued investment in product development and R&D.

“This is an important milestone for us, but the funding itself is not the destination. What matters is what it enables us to build from here,” added Sieber-Gasser.

With geopolitical uncertainty and shifting tariff regimes reordering the global supply chains, the demand for intelligent trade compliance tools is surging with NMSC forecasting the AI trade compliance market to reach €9.84 billion ($11.05 billion) by 2035, expanding at a 21.07% CAGR. Besso is positioning itself as the platform of record for multinationals looking to reduce trade-related costs and build more resilient supply chains.

]]> What does it take to turn university research into a globally competitive startup? And what can Europe and Asia learn from each other when it comes to innovation, investment and emerging technologies?

These questions shaped our visit to Singapore’s A5X conference, where EU-Startups was invited by NUSX, the National University of Singapore’s innovation and enterprise arm, to interview founders, investors and academics about the future of DeepTech.

Across six conversations, alongside interviews with the winners of the Singapore Defense Tech Hackathon, a common theme emerged: scientific breakthroughs alone are not enough. Building successful technology companies requires capital, infrastructure, international collaboration and, crucially, a clearer path from laboratory research to commercial applications.

Click here to watch our onsite interviews.

Beyond the lab

One of A5X’s major developments was the evolution of NUS Enterprise into NUSX, accompanied by ambitions to generate US$1 billion in financial returns and develop technologies capable of positively impacting one billion people by 2035.

For Dr. Tan Sian Wee, Senior Vice President of Innovation and Enterprise at NUS, achieving these goals requires rethinking the earliest stages of venture creation.

Rather than simply investing in existing startups, NUSX wants to identify commercially promising research, validate its market potential and help assemble the teams needed to transform discoveries into businesses.

As Dr. Tan explained: “So it’s really a talent pipeline, a technology pipeline, a capital pipeline and then an impact pipeline. That’s what we’re thinking about step by step by step. So on the talent portion of things, we’ve been operating the National University of Singapore’s overseas colleges programme for over 20 years now. It started with Silicon Valley and we’ve built other locations around the world.”

An important part of this strategy is Nova, NUSX’s newly announced AI platform, designed to analyse university research and identify potential commercial applications, licensing opportunities and industry partnerships.

Professor Benjamin Tee, Vice President of Ecosystem Building at NUSX, reinforced this emphasis on commercialisation. A serial entrepreneur and researcher, Tee discussed the challenges of translating academic discoveries into products, particularly in fields requiring expensive infrastructure and lengthy development cycles.

For Tee, research institutions must increasingly consider the practical outcomes of their work. As he noted: “What is happening today is that there’s a massive change in how we think about research and its impact. Many agencies today are looking at impact both commercially as well as social. The way to bring impact to people is really to take the next step. Going out of your lab, talking to potential people, potential users, and seeing how your technology can fit into their workflow, into their lives.”

Bridging two worlds

International collaboration was another major talking point, particularly following the announcement of a partnership between NUSX and Munich-based UnternehmerTUM.

Professor Helmut Schönenberger, co-founder and CEO of UnternehmerTUM, explained how the organisation has developed a venture-building ecosystem connecting education, research, prototyping, investment and industrial partnerships.

However, he argued that even well-developed local ecosystems cannot provide everything a globally ambitious startup needs.

As Schönenberger put it: “I think every ecosystem has its strengths and then the question is, as an entrepreneur, ‘where do I need a base to really bring the company to the next phase?’ […] If you really want to build a global company today you have to leverage many ecosystems.”

Munich offers access to established industrial networks, engineering expertise and European customers. Singapore, meanwhile, provides connections to Asian markets, research talent and substantial investment resources.

The partnership aims to connect these complementary strengths through international venture-building activities, investment relationships and talent exchanges.

Both Schönenberger and Dr. Tan emphasised that these connections must begin well before startups are ready to expand internationally.

AI’s reality check

Artificial intelligence featured prominently throughout A5X, but the conversations also revealed a distinction between AI’s technological possibilities and the infrastructure required to deliver them.

Dr Orna Berry, Technical Director at Google Cloud and former Chief Scientist of Israel’s Ministry of Industry and Trade, brought decades of experience in entrepreneurship, technology policy and research to the discussion.

Her central message was that advances in AI depend heavily on reliable computing resources, connectivity and energy infrastructure.

As Berry observed: “Infrastructure is always a bottleneck […] I think a great example of building a fairly clean infrastructure is Finland and the Hamina data centres. The first generation was built with significant power based on wind, and the second generation is also built with the ability to distribute heat to to be used in the surrounding.”

Berry also challenged the idea that regulation and innovation are necessarily incompatible. While excessive restrictions can complicate entrepreneurship, technologies used in healthcare, finance and critical infrastructure require safeguards and accountability.

These questions became particularly tangible in our conversation with Dr Babak Parviz, Co-Founder and CEO of NewDays.ai, a Seattle-based startup founded in 2024 that uses AI to support people experiencing dementia and cognitive impairment.

Previously involved in developing Google Glass and leading initiatives at Amazon, Parviz is now applying his experience to a healthcare problem with personal significance.

NewDays combines generative AI with human clinical supervision to make personalised cognitive interventions more accessible. The technology can undertake repetitive elements of treatment while qualified clinicians remain responsible for patient care.

He also highlighted one advantage smaller startups have over technology giants: “I think for a younger company really it boils down to velocity of execution. So either a younger company can execute fast and that’s really what they have. If not they would definitely lose to the larger companies and this is our attempt to execute as fast as possible and be very focused also on one specific problem that we’re trying to solve.”

For NewDays, this means focusing on a specific clinical problem and developing a solution that larger, less specialised organisations might struggle to prioritise.

Defence meets DeepTech

The conference also explored the increasingly important intersection between venture creation and defence innovation.

Gary Ang, Professor of Practice in Defence Innovation and Applications at NUS and founder of the NUS Defence Tech Venture Lab, discussed the challenges of bringing defence technologies from early research into operational environments.

“So this mission that we have here is building building national resilience through defense entrepreneurship. […] So there are two ways to do it, and they complement each other. One is to have a hackathon, because in hackathon you get talent and you convert talent into startups.”

These themes were reflected in the Singapore Defense Tech Hackathon, which brought together teams to develop solutions addressing practical defence challenges.

We also spoke with Wayne Lin of NeuroMech, winner of the 48-hour challenge, whose team developed a brain-computer interface for controlling unmanned ground vehicles, and Vaikesh Manimaran of MAELSTROM, winner of the three-month challenge, whose team worked on a coordinated micro-missile system designed to counter hostile drone swarms.

Both projects illustrated the potential of combining emerging technologies with defence applications, while also raising questions about technical reliability, commercialisation and the role of human oversight in increasingly autonomous systems.

Final Thoughts

Across all these conversations, A5X revealed how closely connected the challenges facing Europe’s and Asia’s innovation ecosystems have become.

Universities need better ways to commercialise research, founders need access to international talent and customers, and investors must support technologies that often require years to reach market readiness.

The growing relationship between NUSX and European institutions such as UnternehmerTUM offers one possible response: building innovation ecosystems that collaborate internationally from the beginning, rather than waiting until startups are ready to expand.

]]> “We’ve validated the idea.” I hear that sentence from founders more than almost any other, and it usually comes with evidence. Thirty people loved it. Two hundred joined the waitlist. In a survey, 80% said they would use it, and a mentor called it a great idea.

It sounds like progress. Most of the time, it isn’t.

When CB Insights reviewed 101 startup post-mortems, 42% of founders said they built something nobody wanted. It was the most common reason for failure in the study. It is also the one cause founders can almost entirely avoid before writing a line of code.

Founders collect opinions about a product that doesn’t exist yet and call it validation. Then they skip the work that would tell them the truth.

Why the yes misleads you

Look at that evidence again. None of it describes something that already happened. It’s all opinion about a future that hasn’t arrived.

People are kind. Ask someone what they think of your idea, and you haven’t asked a research question. You’ve asked them to choose between honesty and your feelings. Most pick your feelings.

Founders also ask leading questions without noticing. “Wouldn’t it be useful if this happened automatically?” Nobody has ever said no to that.

Then there’s cost. A waitlist signup takes an email address and four seconds. A yes that costs nothing proves nothing.

And most founders go looking for a yes. You may have left a job for this idea. So you ask in a way that makes yes easy to say, and once you hear it, you stop asking. That’s confirmation bias, and being clever doesn’t protect you from it. The only defence is a method that stops you from steering the answer.

You can’t validate an idea, only a problem

Your idea is a guess at a solution. Until you build it, nothing in the world can check it. Asking people about it means asking them to imagine a product and predict how they’d behave around it. We’re all bad at that. Ask anyone in January how often they’ll go to the gym in February.

The problem is different. It’s already happening, whether your startup exists or not. Someone is losing an hour a week to it, or paying for a clumsy fix. That’s a fact, and facts can be checked.

That is what customer discovery is for. You hold structured conversations with people who have the problem, and find out whether it’s real, how much it hurts, how often it happens, and whether they already spend time or money on it.

You never need to mention your idea, and you shouldn’t. The moment you describe your solution, people stop telling you about their lives and start reacting to your pitch. Afterwards, you can’t tell the two apart in your notes.

Ask about the last time, not the next time

People don’t lie about their future behaviour, but they’re bad at predicting it. “Would you use this?” gets you a sincere description of the person they intend to be, and you can’t build a business on that.

The past left evidence: spreadsheets, invoices, calendar entries, irritated messages to colleagues. Three questions do most of the work.

  1. Tell me about the last time this happened.
  2. What did you do about it?
  3. What did that cost you, in time, money or something you gave up?

If they can’t remember the last time, the problem isn’t painful enough to be memorable. If they remember it but did nothing, they’re living with it. But if they remember it in detail and built a spreadsheet at 11pm to cope, you’ve found something real. People don’t build workarounds for problems they don’t have.

Define your customer by behaviour, not demographics. “Small business owner” isn’t a customer. “People who send at least five invoices a month and chase the late ones themselves” is.

Leave out anyone who wants you to win, including friends and family. They’ll tell you what you want to hear.

Read the pattern, then decide

For one clearly defined customer type, the same themes usually repeat within eight to 12 conversations. Stop when new conversations stop surprising you.

The strongest signal is the same workaround, invented separately by people who have never met. When two strangers have built the same ugly spreadsheet, you’re looking at a market. Count how many people said something, not how loudly one person said it.

Then make an honest call. If the problem is real, painful, frequent, and already costing people, persevere, and build the smallest thing that tests whether your solution helps. If it’s real but not the problem you expected, or it belongs to a different customer, pivot and take what you learned with you.

If nobody is bleeding, go and find a problem that hurts. Learning that in a few weeks, rather than after 18 months and your savings, is the cheapest good news you’ll ever get.

Decide what a no looks like first

The hard part is making the call before you go looking for one more yes to justify what you already wanted to build.

So before your first conversation, write down what evidence would tell you to stop. The version of you who has done twelve interviews will be more attached to the idea than the version of you reading this. That person shouldn’t be the one setting the bar.

This week, find five people who have the problem and book three conversations. Ask about the last time it happened, and don’t mention your idea.

]]> Brighton-based Universal Quantum, a company building large-scale quantum computing systems for real-world use, today announced it has secured over €89 million ($100 million) in Series A funding – reprotedly marking the largest Series A ever raised by a quantum firm in the UK.

The funding will accelerate the company’s global expansion, as well as the development and commercialisation of its modular technology, advancing a path towards fault-tolerant quantum computing.

The round was co-led by DCVC and Firgun Ventures, with participation from EDBI, Artal, Integral GlobalTech, Main Sequence, Hostplus, NGS Super, IAG Capital, EdenBase, Eigenstate.holdings, and Dave Baszucki (founder and CEO of Roblox), as well as other existing and new strategic investors including Nauta Capital and The Venture Collective.

“Universal Quantum’s progress reflects our partners’ belief that we represent one of the most credible paths to quantum computing at scale,” says Dr. Sebastian Weidt, CEO and co-founder of Universal Quantum. “This round unites an extraordinary group of investors from the world’s most important pools of capital around a single mission: delivering utility-scale quantum computing.”

Universal Quantum’s Series A comes amid continued investment in European quantum computing hardware in 2026.

According to EU-Startups reporting, seven comparable companies have secured approximately €714 million this year, bringing the combined figure to over €803 million including Universal Quantum’s latest round.

In the UK, Oxford Quantum Circuits raised €301 million to expand its Quantum-AI data-centre platform, while Delft-based QuantWare secured €152 million to scale quantum processor manufacturing and France’s Quobly raised €115 million to industrialise silicon-based quantum computers.

Particularly relevant to Universal Quantum’s trapped-ion approach are Germany’s eleQtron, which raised €57 million, and Switzerland’s ZuriQ, which secured €22.4 million.

Firgun Ventures, co-lead investor in Universal Quantum’s round, also participated in the Oxford Quantum Circuits and ZuriQ financings.

EU-Startups previously covered Universal Quantum in June 2020, when the Brighton-based company secured €4 million in Seed funding to develop its modular quantum computing technology.

“Universal Quantum brings together world-class scientific leadership with an exceptionally clear approach to quantum computing,” adds Zeynep Korutürk, Founding & Managing Partner of Firgun Ventures. “Having laid some of the earliest foundations for large-scale trapped-ion architectures, Sebastian and Winfried are true pioneers in the field. With Europe under pressure to prove it can compete on frontier technologies, we are proud to invest in a European company that has grown into a global player, one that is well positioned to help define the future of industrial-scale quantum computing.”

Universal Quantum was founded in 2018 by Professor Sebastian Weidt and Professor Winfried Hensinger of the University of Sussex, co-authors of the first practical blueprint for a large-scale trapped-ion quantum computer, published in 2017.

What began as an academic vision has since become a global engineering operation, with sites across three continents and more than 100 highly technical FTEs.

The company is building utility-scale quantum computers to help confront global challenges. That means reaching the large numbers of high-quality qubits needed to perform real-world tasks, from drug discovery and battery design to climate modelling and many others beyond the reach of classical computers.

Its modular trapped-ion architecture and enabling technologies are designed to make this achievable.

Today’s new capital will drive the continued development and commercialisation of Universal Quantum’s modular approach to building the quantum computers needed for practical, error-corrected use.

The company looks to leverage their patented, world-record interconnect technology and advanced integrated chips to develop the chiplet arrays and control systems required to reduce engineering risk and accelerate the path to larger-scale quantum computers.

The funding will also support Universal Quantum’s recently announced expansion in Singapore, where it is establishing its first R&D centre outside Europe, as well as expansion in the United States, Japan and across its German hub in Hamburg.

“True quantum utility will be unlocked by companies that are relentlessly focused on the scalability of their machines,” says James Hardiman, General Partner at DCVC. “Universal Quantum’s modular architecture addresses the hardest challenges in scaling ion trap systems. Quantum is a global race, and we are pleased to back a team with genuine standing across Europe, Asia-Pacific and North America.”

Each chip uses trapped-ion technology, where charged atoms held in place by electric fields act as qubits. Universal Quantum’s approach is designed to connect these modules in a practical, manufacturable way, creating a route to the scale needed for fault-tolerant quantum computing and giving industry partners a clearer path to quantum utility.

According to data provided by the company, the quantum technology market could be worth €53-89 billion ($60-100 billion) annually by 2035, while helping to unlock up to €2.4 trillion ($2.7 trillion) of economic value worldwide in sectors such as pharmaceuticals, finance and automotive.

“What sets Universal Quantum apart is its ability to win major contracts at this stage of development,” adds Bill Bartee, Managing Partner at Main Sequence. “In a sector where hype and hyperbole are running far ahead of commercial reality, Universal Quantum has built a paying customer base that includes some of the world’s most demanding scientific and government institutions, and has done so before most competitors have shipped any working hardware.”

Now delivering against a €68 million ($77 million) contract with the German Aerospace Center (DLR), Universal Quantum is establishing a permanent presence via an R&D centre in Singapore, with further international collaborations to be announced soon.

Citing Goldman Sachs research forecasting that the global commercial robotaxi market could reach roughly €365 billion by 2035, with a fleet of around six million vehicles, NeoFleet opines that this growth will also create a much larger institutional asset class around mobility infrastructure.

“A vehicle generates income for a driver every day. This helps move them from poverty towards middle-income earnings, increases access to mobility for passengers, and ultimately supports the wider economy. At the same time, enormous pools of institutional capital are looking for attractive, asset-backed returns but have no scalable way of reaching these fragmented markets. NeoFleet is building the infrastructure that bridges that gap,” added Loughran. 

The firm’s leadership team includes two inDrive alumni: Loughran and CEO Igor Shiyanov, who founded NeoFleet after building and selling a delivery startup to a ride-hailing operator. Shiyanov also previously worked at inDrive and Boston Consulting Group.

Co-founder Oleg Mosyazh leads business development and capital raising, and previously worked at Microsoft and PwC.

The company plans to use this capital to enter additional high-growth mobility markets across Africa, Latin America, and Asia. By the end of 2027, NeoFleet aims to support approximately 5,000 vehicles across its network, representing an estimated €65–87 million in vehicle value.

The firm notes that this expansion is intended to establish the operating, financing, and technology infrastructure required for NeoFleet’s longer-term ambition: becoming a major global capital and fleet-management platform for both human-driven and autonomous mobility.

Just two weeks after it was launched, the Copernicus Sentinel-3C satellite returned its first images and measurements from two of its key instruments – a major milestone that confirms the satellite is working well and on the road to monitoring the health of Earth’s oceans, land, cryosphere and atmosphere.

]]> 29aea361935aecd30ce0373f24bf62f8 Thu, 08 Oct 2026 14:25:00 +0200 Solar Orbiter tracks origin of mysterious magnetic switchbacks

The European Space Agency-led Solar Orbiter spacecraft has flown through an S-shaped kink known as a ‘switchback’ in the solar wind’s magnetic field. By fingerprinting the elusive particles within the switchback, Solar Orbiter has traced its origin back to the Sun’s surface and revealed more about solar magnetism – the unruly instigator of dangerous solar storms.

]]> 4f12735247a3bacad39d5964e4ae8495 Thu, 08 Oct 2026 11:00:00 +0200 Keeping the sky dark and quiet

For thousands of years, the night sky has inspired humanity, guided explorers and helped scientists unlock the mysteries of the Universe. As the number of satellites in orbit grows, their reflected light and radio frequency interference become a challenge for both professional astronomy and simple stargazing.

The European Space Agency (ESA) and the International Astronomical Union’s Centre for the Protection of the Dark and Quiet Sky (IAU CPS) have signed an agreement at the International Astronautical Congress to strengthen cooperation and develop technical solutions to keep the sky dark and quiet.

]]> 465710a60db91246609d764ac15e565e Thu, 08 Oct 2026 10:00:00 +0200 The Incredible Adventures of the Hera mission – The space detectives arrive Video: 00:04:19

Meet Hera, our very own asteroid detective. Together with two CubeSats – Milani the rock decoder and Juventas the radar visionary – Hera is off on an adventure to explore Didymos, a double asteroid system that is typical of the thousands that pose an impact risk to planet Earth.

After their two year cosmic roadtrip, Hera and its little CubeSat companions have finally arrived at Didymos and Dimorphos – the very first Solar System object to have had its orbit shifted by human action.  Suitable for kids and adults alike, this episode of ‘The Incredible Adventures of the Hera mission’ explains what ESA’s asteroid detective and its CubeSat assistants will be up to once they arrive, and precisely how they are going to say goodbye to each other – letting the CubeSats begin their close-up exam of this historic space rock.

<!DOCTYPE html><html lang="en-US"><head><meta charset="UTF-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"><link rel="pingback" href="https://www.studyineurope.eu/xmlrpc.php"> <style id="sie-lean-layout"> #sie-lean-main { margin: 0; }
 #sie-lean-main > *:first-child,
 #sie-lean-main .sie-field-page { margin-top: 0; }
 .et_builder_inner_content { width: 100%; }
 .et_pb_section { position: relative; }
 .et_pb_row { position: relative; width: 80%; max-width: 1080px; margin: 0 auto; }
 .et_pb_row_inner { width: 100%; }
 .et_pb_column { position: relative; } </style> <style id="sie-custom-header-inline">/* ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
 SIE Custom Header — v1.1.2
 Zero-CLS, no JavaScript layout shifts.
 No panoramic image — lean 64px nav bar only.
 backdrop-filter is intentionally NOT used on .sie-hdr__bar.
 Any element with backdrop-filter becomes a CSS containing block for
 position:fixed descendants, which would trap the user-ui mobile bottom bar
 (position:fixed; bottom:0) inside the header instead of the viewport.
 ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ */
/* ── Root variables ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
:root {
 --sie-hdr-brand:       #0056b3;        /* SIE brand blue                      */
 --sie-hdr-brand-light: #1a6fc4;
 --sie-hdr-bar-h:       64px;           /* nav bar height — fixed, prevents CLS */
 --sie-hdr-bar-bg:      #0056b3;        /* solid — no backdrop-filter needed   */
 --sie-hdr-bar-border:  rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.15);
}
/* ── Wrapper ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr {
 width: 100%;
 display: block;
 min-height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 /* Own stacking context so dropdowns render above Divi page content */
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1000;
}
/* ── Navigation bar ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__bar {
 height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 background: var(--sie-hdr-bar-bg);
 /* NO backdrop-filter here — it would trap position:fixed children
 (user-ui mobile bottom bar) inside this element instead of viewport */
 border-bottom: 1px solid var(--sie-hdr-bar-border);
}
.sie-hdr__inner {
 max-width: 1280px;
 height: 100%;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 24px;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 32px;
}
/* ── Logo ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__logo {
 flex-shrink: 0;
 text-decoration: none;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-img {
 height: 54px;
 width: auto;
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-text {
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 17px;
 font-weight: 700;
 color: #fff;
 letter-spacing: -0.01em;
 white-space: nowrap;
}
/* ── Desktop navigation ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__nav {
 flex: 1;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list {
 list-style: none;
 margin: 0;
 padding: 0;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list li {
 position: relative;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
 padding: 8px 14px;
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 text-decoration: none;
 border-radius: 8px;
 transition: background 0.15s ease, color 0.15s ease;
 white-space: nowrap;
 min-height: 48px; /* WCAG touch target */
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a:hover,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle:hover,
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover > .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 color: #fff;
}
/* ── Resources dropdown ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: none;
 position: absolute;
 top: calc(100% + 6px);
 left: 0;
 min-width: 240px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 12px;
 box-shadow: 0 12px 40px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.18);
 padding: 8px 0;
 list-style: none;
 margin: 0;
 z-index: 9999;
}
/* CSS-only hover on desktop */
@media (hover: hover) {
 .sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover > .sie-hdr__dropdown,
 .sie-hdr__has-dropdown:focus-within > .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: block;
 }
}
/* JS-toggled state (mobile / keyboard) */
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown.is-open > .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown li {
 margin: 0;
 padding: 0;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown a {
 display: block;
 padding: 10px 18px;
 font-size: 13.5px;
 color: #003B73;
 font-weight: 500;
 border-radius: 0;
 min-height: unset;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown a:hover {
 background: #f0f7ff;
 color: #0b5394;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg {
 transition: transform 0.2s ease;
}
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown.is-open .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg,
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg {
 transform: rotate(180deg);
}
/* ── Mobile hamburger ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__hamburger {
 display: none;
 flex-direction: column;
 justify-content: center;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 5px;
 width: 44px;
 height: 44px;
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 0;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 margin-left: auto;
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger span {
 display: block;
 width: 22px;
 height: 2px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 2px;
 transition: transform 0.25s ease, opacity 0.25s ease;
}
/* Animate to ✕ when open */
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(1) {
 transform: translateY(7px) rotate(45deg);
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(2) {
 opacity: 0;
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(3) {
 transform: translateY(-7px) rotate(-45deg);
}
/* ── User-UI icon bar integration ────────────────────────────────────────────
 user-ui.php's desktop bar uses position:absolute; top:20px; right:30px — that
 was designed for Divi's header context. Inside our flex .sie-hdr__inner we
 need it as a normal flex child instead.
 Fixed-position children (auth drawer, mobile bar, destinations panel) are
 unaffected — position:fixed is always viewport-relative provided no ancestor
 has backdrop-filter, transform, or perspective (we intentionally avoid all
 three on .sie-hdr__bar).
 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 position: static !important;
 top: auto !important;
 right: auto !important;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 margin-left: auto;
}
/* Align our mobile breakpoint (860px) with user-ui's desktop/mobile split */
@media (min-width: 861px) {
 .sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 display: flex !important;
 }
}
@media (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 display: none !important;
 }
}
/* Leonardo icon in the nav bar.
 user-ui's default .se-ai-icon is 86×86 px (fine for the mobile bottom bar),
 but that overflows our 64px-tall nav bar. Override to a crisp 36px square —
 the webp source is already high-res so it stays sharp at 2× on retina. */
.sie-hdr .se-ai-icon {
 width:  36px !important;
 height: 36px !important;
 border-radius: 50%;
 object-fit: cover;
}
/* Icon colours inside the header.
 user-ui defaults: map icon is #2f6fed (dark blue) and heart is #F44336 (red).
 The map icon is nearly invisible on our #0056b3 bar — lift all icons to white.
 The heart keeps its red via the !important below so favourited items still pop. */
.sie-hdr .se-shortlist-link,
.sie-hdr .se-dest-desktop-btn,
.sie-hdr .se-user-icon {
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.85) !important;
}
.sie-hdr .se-shortlist-link:hover,
.sie-hdr .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover,
.sie-hdr .se-user-icon:hover {
 color: #fff !important;
}
/* Fav heart — keep the red so it reads as "save" */
.sie-hdr .se-fav-desktop-link {
 color: #ff6b6b !important;   /* slightly lighter red, readable on blue */
}
.sie-hdr .se-fav-desktop-link:hover {
 color: #ff4444 !important;
}
/* ── Responsive ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
@media (max-width: 860px) {
 :root {
 --sie-hdr-bar-h: 56px;
 }
 .sie-hdr {
 min-height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 }
 .sie-hdr__hamburger {
 display: flex;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav {
 /* Hidden off-screen when closed — no layout shift */
 position: absolute;
 top: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);           /* flush below the nav bar */
 left: 0;
 right: 0;
 background: var(--sie-hdr-bar-bg);
 /* NO backdrop-filter — same reason as .sie-hdr__bar */
 padding: 12px 0 20px;
 clip-path: inset(0 0 100% 0);       /* collapses upward — no CLS */
 transition: clip-path 0.3s ease;
 z-index: 9998;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav.is-open {
 clip-path: inset(0);
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav-list {
 flex-direction: column;
 align-items: flex-start;
 gap: 0;
 padding: 0 16px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav-list a,
 .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 width: 100%;
 font-size: 15px;
 padding: 12px 8px;
 border-radius: 8px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 position: static;
 box-shadow: none;
 border-radius: 0;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.06);
 padding: 4px 0 4px 16px;
 margin: 4px 0;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown a {
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.8);
 font-size: 14px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown a:hover {
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.08);
 color: #fff;
 }
}
@media (max-width: 480px) {
 .sie-hdr__inner {
 padding: 0 16px;
 gap: 16px;
 }
}
/* Hover-gap fix: invisible bridge spanning the 6px gap between the nav item
 and the dropdown panel, so the cursor never "leaves" while crossing. */
.sie-hdr__dropdown::before {
 content: "";
 position: absolute;
 top: -10px;
 left: 0;
 right: 0;
 height: 10px;
}
/* Anti-FOUC guard for body-rendered overlays: their own CSS arrives 20KB+
 later in the HTML stream, so on slow connections they paint fully visible
 (the destinations grid "opens" during load). Force the CLOSED state from
 first paint — each component's .open/.is-open rules override these. */
.sie-dest-panel,
#sie-auth-drawer,
#sie-lead-form-drawer,
.sie-finder-overlay {
 position: fixed;
 inset: 0;
 opacity: 0;
 visibility: hidden;
} </style> <style id="sie-etmodules-font-display">@font-face{font-family:"ETmodules";src:url("https://www.studyineurope.eu/core/views/sie-theme/css/base/modules.woff") format("woff");font-style:normal;font-weight:normal;font-display:swap;}</style><meta name='robots' content='index, follow, max-image-preview:large, max-snippet:-1, max-video-preview:-1' /> <style id="sie-hide-divi-header"> /* Hide Divi's header (Theme Builder + classic) */

<span><span>sandoel</span></span>

<div class="ecl"><h2><strong>What is the Conference?</strong></h2>

<p>The <strong>Conference on the Future of Europe </strong>is the first transnational discussion with Europeans on how to address Europe’s challenges together. This is an opportunity to think about what citizens and&nbsp; civil society want for the European Union.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

  <div class="eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text"><h2><strong>How does the Conference work?</strong></h2>

<p>Europeans can share ideas via the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Multilingual Digital Platform</a>, and both national and&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/assemblies/citizens-panels" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">European Citizens' Panels</a>. These contributions feed into the&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/plenary" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference Plenaries</a>.</p>

<p>The Conference&nbsp;offers a new public forum for an open, inclusive, and transparent debate with citizens around a number of key priorities and challenges.</p>

<h2><strong>How can you participate?</strong></h2>

<ul>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]--><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/processes?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">share your own ideas or support others’ ideas</a> on the multilingual digital Conference platform</li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->organise your own events and promote it by adding them to the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference platform</a></li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->take a look at the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/meetings" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">events organised by people across the EU</a></li>
</ul>

<h2><strong>What will the outcome be?</strong></h2>

<p>All of the ideas gathered and reports on events are published on the platform openly and transparently. These reports will then directly influence the discussions in the European Citizens’ Panels as well as in the Plenaries, where citizens will enter into a dialogue with national and European decision makers.</p>

<p>By spring 2022, the Conference will provide guidance on the future of Europe to the European institutions</p>

<p><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/getinvolved" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Get involved and make your voice heard when it comes to education, culture, youth, sport, and more</a>.</p>

<item>
  <title>European Student Card Initiative at EAIE 2026 in Glasgow - main highlights</title>
  <link>https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/european-student-card-initiative/news/european-student-card-initiative-at-eaie-2026-in-glasgow-main-highlights</link>
  <description>
<h1 class="title-h1 eac-page-title">European Student Card Initiative at EAIE 2026 in Glasgow - main highlights</h1>
<span><span>holbobe</span></span>
<span><time datetime="2026-09-30T09:11:45+02:00" title="Wednesday, September 30, 2026 - 09:11">Wed, 09/30/2026 - 09:11</time>
</span>
<div class="ecl"><p>EAIE 2026 took place from 8 to 11 September, with this year’s theme being “The Rhythm of Revolution”. ESCI featured in five activities: two sessions in the main conference programme and three mini-sessions at the European Commission stand.</p><h2>Shaping the next phase of the ESCI</h2><p>The session “What’s next for the European Student Card Initiative?” brought together Victor Aguilar Mendez from the European Commission, Harpa Sif Arnarsdóttir from RANNIS and Sergi Martínez Rigol from the University of Barcelona to discuss the roadmap beyond 2027.</p><p>The discussion highlighted three main points:</p><ul><li data-list-item-id="ec04a08fab5a0a15faf6d0537ff166c1e"><strong>Build on strong foundations</strong>. Participants welcomed the ambition to further simplify student mobility and emphasised the importance of building on the progress already achieved. They also noted that digital transformation involves more than technical connections, requiring aligned processes, staff capacity and resources.</li><li data-list-item-id="ec8f6683d0b4c64c36760e88ede263ada"><strong>Give institutions clarity and time to prepare</strong>. Participants highlighted the value of clear information on the <a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/european-student-card-initiative/about/esci-2028-2034/continuity-and-preparation?">future scope of ESCI+</a>, practical implications and transition arrangements. The European Commission indicated that 2028 and 2029 are envisaged as transition years.</li><li data-list-item-id="e8a2629faf233a9053a3e7c84c25e2248"><strong>Broaden engagement beyond international relations and IT teams</strong>. Participants highlighted the value of involving university leadership, national authorities, governance bodies and research and education networks.</li></ul><h2>Practical exchange at the European Commission stand</h2><p>Three mini-sessions created space for practical discussion and peer exchange at the European Commission stand:</p><ul><li data-list-item-id="ea46800eaa0963f636bf8742a636fe844"><strong>Digital Officers and ESCI Champions</strong>: “Meet and Greet” explored different opportunities for close collaboration and participants discussed faster communication channels, technical sub-groups and ways to strengthen the community of practitioners.</li><li data-list-item-id="e722608eb7be29071793748afb04db370"><strong>ESCI+ timeline: what to expect and when</strong>, focused on preparations in 2026 and plans for 2027. Participants asked for timely communication, hands-on training, transition arrangements and support to integrate future developments with existing systems.</li><li data-list-item-id="e4abeb75d22c4e87d628dd3a9174bdc0a"><strong>How to issue your first European Student Card</strong> introduced the practical tools available to card issuers, including the ESC Router and the ESC Service Manager for listing services available to ESC holders.</li></ul><h2>Poster session: “The European Student Card: Bridging borders for students”</h2><p>The poster attracted strong interest, with ESCI representatives Elodie Ham (EACEA) and Deborah Arnold (NTT DATA) engaging with participants on the ESCI components and discussing the implications of the ESCI+ timeline with those already involved in the initiative as well as with potential newcomers.</p><h2>Session by ESCI Champions: “Erasmus Without Paper: Getting on board with the digitisation of Erasmus+"&nbsp;</h2></div>
<div class="ecl-u-type-bold ecl-u-mb-m">Intro Text</div><div class="eac-hero"><p>We joined more than 7,300 international education professionals from over 100 countries in Glasgow to discuss what comes next for the European Student Card Initiative and share practical guidance with institutions.</p></div>

                    <div class="eche-report-title-question-text-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution has a strategy and an overarching structure supporting internationalisation</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>
                    </div>
                </div>
                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">
                    <div class="eche-report-border"></div>
                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The internationalisation strategy is available and prominently displayed on your website</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Internationalisation is an important driver for institutional change, and has a great influence on the major activities of a higher education institution (HEI) i.e. education and research. The importance of internationalisation is recognised, and most institutions have a strategy for internationalisation. However, for a strategy to be efficient, and for it to drive the HEI's activities regarding internationalisation, there is a need for its acceptance from across the whole institution. In addition the strategy could also be accessible to external collaborative partners. It is highly important to have the institution's internationalisation and modernisation strategy published and easily accessible to all.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The institution has a clear plan to implement the strategy</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The strategy and policy should include explicit allocation of responsibilities for its efficient implementation to individuals at all levels of the institution, from senior management to the heads of departments, schools and faculties, to academic and administrative staff. This will ensure acceptance and accountability for the strategy. The internationalisation strategy and policy should outline a specific implementation plan that sets out explicitly the financial and human resources available.&nbsp; For example, it is recommended to set up an International Relations Office (IRO) to implement mobility and other international projects.</p><p>As with any other activity, the institutional implementation of the internationalisation strategy is dependent on the people behind the activities. It is highly important for an institution to have staff with the right set of skills and knowledge driving the internationalisation agenda and liaising with international students and staff members. Therefore understanding the development needs of the staff and supporting their professional development should be a high priority for the institution. Such development should focus on both staff engaged in international activities as well as the supporting staff, ensuring the most efficient implementation of international activities and cooperative projects across the institution. For example, trainings/webinars/projects could be organised on intercultural competences and communication, project management, enhancement of internationalisation at home/intercultural, or other activities suggested by the staff and supported by the hierarchy.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes incoming and outgoing student and staff mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Mobility is important to the development of the institution as a whole as well as for the individual participants. Therefore the HEI should make mobility and international cooperation a central element in its institutional policies, and explicitly and consistently promote and support student and staff mobility. Non-discrimination policies and further emphasis on the promotion of mobility for under-represented groups should also form an integral part of the institutional support structures.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes engagement in European and international cooperation projects</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution's internationalisation strategy and policy should explicitly and consistently promote the development of cooperation with partners in other EU and non-EU countries. The activities and co-operation projects agreed by the HEI should be based on identified needs. In addition they should identify geographical and subject priorities of the internationalisation strategy.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The implementation of the strategic plan is monitored</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>International activity, including co-operation projects and mobility should be carefully monitored. Clear and unambiguous monitoring of such activity are key to ensuring success. Explicit indicators should be developed to show specific success scenarios. The indicators should be SMART.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Incentives are provided to staff involved in international activities</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Participation in such international projects should be seen as an important aspect of the professional development of the staff and of the modernisation of the HEI. It should, therefore, be considered a key component in staff evaluation. As part of the institutional modernisation and internationalisation strategy, concrete support measures should be defined at both institutional and departmental levels to encourage and recognise staff participating in such projects, as well as allow adequate time to carry out this work.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-case">

                                             </div>

                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>In signing the Erasmus Charter for Higher Education, the institution agrees to respect <strong>in full</strong> the principles of non-discrimination as set out in the Programme. The institution must clearly demonstrate through its policies, rules and regulations that equal access and opportunities to mobile participants from all backgrounds. Which means that all individuals or groups will be treated equally, irrespective of their characteristics. In accordance with Article 21 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, there should be no discrimination "based on sex, race, colour, ethnic or social origin, genetic features, language, religion or belief, political or any other opinion, membership of a national minority, property, birth, disability, age or sexual orientation". For more information, see: <a href="http://www.europarl.europa.eu/charter/pdf/text_en.pdf">http://www.europarl.europa.eu/charter/pdf/text_en.pdf</a></p>                      </div>

                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Ensuring that the mobile participant, sending and receiving HEI/organisation/enterprise (i.e. all three parties) sign the Learning Agreement before the start of the mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The purpose of the Learning Agreement is to provide a transparent and efficient preparation of the study period abroad and to ensure that the student will receive recognition in his/her degree for the educational components or traineeship successfully completed abroad. The Learning Agreement:</p><ul><li>Sets out the learning outcomes for the mobility, including both the educational components or traineeship activities to be carried out by the student at the receiving institution/organisation/enterprise, which will be recognised by the sending institution upon successful completion of the study programme abroad and counted towards his/her degree.</li><li>Ensures full recognition for satisfactorily completed activities of study mobility and traineeships in terms of credits awarded, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams, and documents these credits in the student records, so that they can be identified in a transparent way.</li></ul><p>The Learning Agreement is binding for all parties and constitutes the cornerstone of successful student mobility (for studies, traineeships, and combinations thereof), including quality assurances and the process for transparent transfer of credits. Therefore, it is essential to conduct mobility based on an agreed and signed Learning Agreement. It is not compulsory to circulate papers with original signatures; scanned copies of signatures or digital signatures may be accepted, depending on the national legislation.</p><p>The EU official templates for Learning Agreements for studies and traineeships are available online: <a href="http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm">http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm&nbsp;&nbsp;</a></p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Including allocation of responsibility to an academic who has the authority to approve, amend and recognise the Learning Agreements on behalf of the responsible academic body</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The formal procedures for recognising student mobility should clearly and unambiguously set out the responsibilities of an appointed academic, who has the authority, on behalf of the appropriate academic body, to:</p><ul><li>Approve the Learning Agreements,</li><li>Exceptionally amend the Learning Agreements, and</li><li>Recognise the successfully completed activities, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams.</li></ul>                      </div>

                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Ensuring that the mobile participant, sending and receiving HEI/organisation/enterprise (i.e. all three parties) sign the Learning Agreement before the start of the mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The purpose of the Learning Agreement is to provide a transparent and efficient preparation of the study period abroad and to ensure that the student will receive recognition in his/her degree for the educational components or traineeship successfully completed abroad. The Learning Agreement:</p><ul><li>Sets out the learning outcomes for the mobility, including both the educational components or traineeship activities to be carried out by the student at the receiving institution/organisation/enterprise, which will be recognised by the sending institution upon successful completion of the study programme abroad and counted towards his/her degree.</li><li>Ensures full recognition for satisfactorily completed activities of study mobility and traineeships in terms of credits awarded, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams, and documents these credits in the student records, so that they can be identified in a transparent way.</li></ul><p>The Learning Agreement is binding for all parties and constitutes the cornerstone of successful student mobility (for studies, traineeships, and combinations thereof), including quality assurances and the process for transparent transfer of credits.                                                 <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Ensuring that the mobile participant, sending and receiving institution/organisation/enterprise (i.e. all three parties) sign the mobility agreement before the start of the mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>To ensure effective staff mobility, it has to be based on a signed mobility agreement. The mobility agreement has to acceptable and signed by all parties in advance. There are four key elements set out by the mobility agreement, which are intended to increase the relevance and potential impact of the mobility. These are:</p><ul><li>The overall objectives and academic rationale of the mobility,</li><li>The institutional requirements or strategy, and the mobility's added value in the context of modernisation and internationalisation,</li><li>The activities or teaching programme content to be undertaken by the staff member, and,</li><li>The expected outcomes and impact of the mobility on the professional development of the staff member at both institutions.</li></ul><p>For this to work effectively, there needs to be dialogue and discussion between the three parties prior to the signing of the mobility agreement having agreed the common goals which are acceptable.&nbsp;</p>                      </div>

        <div class="eche-report-section-wrapper">
